data.topic: The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

read.lede: The most damaging evidence against Alferd Packer is not that he ate the men. He admitted that. It is that the bodies did not fit his explanation—and that, more than a century later, forensic investigators still disagreed about what those bones could prove. The eleven supplied entries are not eleven independent reconstructions: one is an archive catalogue rather than a narrative, while the long Colorado Encyclopedia entry appears four times at different reading levels. The remaining accounts largely repeat the public record: six prospectors entered the winter mountains, five died, Packer emerged alone, admitted cannibalism while denying murder, escaped, was convicted, and was later paroled after Polly Pry campaigned for him. No account offers a wholly separate eyewitness reconstruction of the killings. The strongest primary material is the surviving paper trail—Packer’s confessions and letters, court files, parole records, and Supreme Court case files—held with penitentiary and military records by the Colorado State Archives, alongside later examination of the remains. Packer’s reckless promise set the expedition on course. In late 1873, he joined roughly twenty gold seekers traveling from Utah toward Colorado’s goldfields after claiming he knew the route. People who knew him described him as argumentative, dishonest, greedy, lazy, and prone to getting lost; he had worked briefly as a guide, but not well. The party struggled through snow, lost the trail, exhausted its provisions, and resorted to horse feed. At Chief Ouray’s camp near Montrose, the starving prospectors received food and shelter, and Ouray warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing in such weather. He offered to let them remain through winter and gave the departing men provisions and directions toward the Los Pinos Agency by way of the Gunnison River. Packer argued instead for the direct mountain route. Five men followed him: Israel Swan, George Noon, Frank Miller, James Humphrey, and Shannon Wilson Bell. They left on February 9, 1874, with food for roughly two weeks, inadequate clothing, almost no matches, no snowshoes, and only a few firearms and tools. Packer reached the agency alone on April 16, after 65 days in the mountains. He arrived in rags, with cloth around his feet, a rifle, a knife, a coffee pot, and a beard, but did not look starved. Although he vomited when first fed, he soon drank whiskey, traveled to Saguache, spent over $100 at Dolan’s saloon on gambling and liquor, bought a $70 horse, spent another $78 at a general store, and made further purchases. Penniless when he joined the expedition, he now carried cash—apparently in different wallets—and possessed a missing man’s rifle and Frank Miller’s knife. Packer first said the others had abandoned him while he warmed frozen feet and that he survived on roots, rosebuds, rabbits, and moccasin leather. The surviving prospectors rejected this: the men would not have abandoned their guide, and the rifle and possessions made his account implausible. When Ute hunters brought human flesh found near the agency, Packer panicked and offered a sworn confession transcribed by clerk Herman Lauter. He said the men had first eaten those who died from hunger or exposure, that Bell killed some of the others, and that Packer killed Bell in self-defense before living on the bodies for nearly sixty days. Packer gave three principal confessions—May 1874, March 1883, and a 1897 letter—and varied the sequence. In one version, Swan and Humphrey died naturally, Miller was killed while Packer gathered wood, Bell shot Noon, and Packer shot Bell. In another, Bell killed the entire camp while Packer scouted, then attacked him with a hatchet. In his later account, Bell was roasting Miller’s flesh when Packer returned, charged him, and was shot and finished with a hatchet. The evidence suggested that Packer killed the men before absolute starvation, then returned to their bodies; cannibalism itself did not prove murder. In August, illustrator John A. Randolph of Harper’s Weekly, an illustrator for Harper’s Weekly, discovered all five bodies together in a pine-shaded gulch near the Lake Fork of the Gunnison, later called Dead Man’s Gulch. Finding them in one place contradicted Packer’s claim that they died separately and were left in different places. The remains showed severe violence: blows fractured skulls, Miller’s head was missing, and flesh had been removed in ways that appeared to exceed animal scavenging. Cloth tied around the feet suggested the men had eaten their shoes, and a path connected the bodies to a crude shelter where Packer had apparently stayed. A broken rifle lay nearby. People therefore developed a stark theory: Packer killed the men for their possessions before supplies were gone, became trapped by snow, and returned to the bodies for meat. The prosecution used the same logic. Hunters testified that deer, antelope, rabbits, and other game remained even in severe winter. Packer’s decision to abandon Ouray’s safer route looked, at minimum, grossly negligent and, at worst, deliberate. The case was that killings preceded absolute starvation, while Packer’s changing accounts and possession of money made robbery a motive. The evidence supports a narrower conclusion than either camp prefers: Bell was probably shot, Packer probably ate the bodies, and deliberate violence is plausible without every part of the prosecution’s theory being proved.

paragraphs.label: Forensic dispute
paragraphs.text: James Starrs, the forensic law professor who led the July 17, 1989, exhumation, declared Packer “guilty as sin.” His team reported blunt-force trauma and extensive knife marks, and Starrs believed Packer initially killed the men to steal their belongings before using their bodies as food. The later account in the pile describes three skeletons with defensive hacking marks on the forearms, including Bell’s, suggesting that some victims may have raised their arms against an attacker. That is difficult to reconcile with Packer’s claim that Bell alone became violent and simply killed the others while they slept. The Colorado Encyclopedia’s reconstruction proposes that Packer bludgeoned two men in their sleep, shot others in the hips to disable them, then killed them with a hatchet. It acknowledges, however, that differing decomposition states complicate the theory and that pelvic punctures might be animal marks. Starrs conceded that nobody could directly prove cannibalism: eating human flesh leaves no simple definitive signature, so his conclusion concerned murder, not eating. Walter Birkby, the forensic anthropologist who worked with Starrs, took the opposite position: “We found nothing to corroborate or refute anything Packer said. We’ll never know who did it based on any solid physical evidence.” Michelle Pierce, drawing on archival research, likewise saw Packer less as a calculating killer than a frightened, socially damaged man whose epilepsy and reputation shaped contemporaries’ judgments. The strongest support for Packer came from David Bailey’s separate investigation. A Colt revolver found at the site in the 1950s, rediscovered in a museum collection in 1994, still held three .38-caliber bullets. Richard Dujay’s electron-microscope analysis at Mesa State College matched their lead composition to fragments recovered from Bell’s remains, and a test with a similar pistol produced a hole like the mark in Bell’s hip. That supports Packer’s claim that he shot Bell, but not self-defense or the injuries to the others. Bailey treated it as vindication, but local historian Grant Houston and even Pierce remained skeptical because people routinely found old guns and bullets near the site and claimed them as Packer relics.

paragraphs.label: Trials and parole
paragraphs.text: Packer’s legal fate depended as much on credibility and the atmosphere around the case as on the remains. He escaped the Saguache jail in 1874, lived under the name John Schwartze, and was captured in Wyoming on March 11, 1883, after nine years on the run. During the investigation before his escape, he also attempted to attack agency clerk Herman Lauter with a knife, an episode that helped convince General Adams that he was dangerous. At his first trial, Packer rambled for six hours, admitted eating the men, and insisted Bell was responsible for the other deaths. The jury convicted him of premeditated murder and sentenced him to hang, but Colorado’s Supreme Court overturned the conviction in October 1885 because the applicable murder statute had been repealed and could not be applied ex post facto to a pre-statehood crime. At his second trial in Gunnison, on June 8, 1886, the jury convicted him on five counts of voluntary manslaughter, and he received forty years—eight years per victim, then the longest prison sentence in U.S. history. He appealed repeatedly and maintained that he had killed only Bell in self-defense. Polly Pry, the Denver Post reporter whose real name was Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan and who became the paper’s first female reporter, turned that claim into a public campaign after visiting him in prison. She portrayed him as an ex-soldier and victim of circumstance; supporters argued that extreme privation blurred responsibility and insanity. Governor Charles Thomas granted parole, not a pardon, on February 8, 1901, after Packer had served about eighteen years. The sources differ on whether the decisive campaign began with Pry, an earlier petitioner named Duane Hatch, or both. The famous story that Judge Melville Gerry sentenced him with the line about eating five of seven Democrats is apocryphal; the surviving court wording is formal and ends only with “dead, dead, dead.” Packer later worked as a Denver Post guard, prospecting again near Littleton, and died in 1907.

paragraphs.label: What remains unknown
paragraphs.text: The decisive piece everyone wants is still missing: a physical reconstruction establishing who struck each blow, when the men died, and whether Bell’s shooting was defensive. No source provides a complete forensic dataset, a conclusive explanation of the pelvic punctures, or evidence resolving the conflicting decomposition patterns. The archive contains confessions, letters, court records, parole files, penitentiary records, and Supreme Court cases, but those records are not examined in full here. No surviving account comes from anyone who witnessed the final camp, and no independent source resolves whether Packer was an incompetent guide whose companions died in catastrophe, a robber who created the catastrophe, or a killer who used genuine starvation to conceal it. The legend remains more complicated than either side’s preferred version: Packer was almost certainly a cannibal, almost certainly lied, and may have killed some or all of the men. The sources do not honestly establish the certainty claimed by either “guilty as sin” or “innocent survivor.”

players.name: Denver Post
players.role: Denver newspaper that published Polly Pry’s campaign for Packer’s release
players.body: The Denver Post employed Polly Pry, who portrayed Packer as an ex-soldier and common man forced into cannibalism to survive. After Packer’s seventeen years in prison, the newspaper petitioned for his release, and Packer later worked there as a guard. Many believed Pry and her employers helped secure both his release and the job. The paper’s complete historical run is also among the Denver Public Library’s research holdings.

players.name: Polly Pry
players.role: Denver Post reporter who campaigned for Packer’s release
players.body: Polly Pry partly believed Packer’s account and portrayed him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment who had survived unimaginable horrors. After noticing Hatch’s decade-long petition effort, she visited Packer at the Colorado State Penitentiary in 1899 and launched a media campaign arguing that he had been unjustly tried and convicted. Packer respected her and called her his “Liberator”; many believed her influence helped obtain his release and his later job at the Denver Post. Polly Pry was the pen name of Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan.

players.name: Israel Swan
players.role: Elderly member of Packer’s five-man prospecting group and alleged first victim
players.body: Packer said Swan died from hunger and exposure, then gave him a rifle before the others abandoned him. In another account, Packer returned from gathering firewood to find the other four men around Swan’s slain body, which Packer said had been struck with a hatchet. He said the men found several thousand dollars on Swan, butchered and ate him, and divided his money. Swan recurs because the conflicting accounts of his death, the rifle, and the missing money are central to the case.

players.name: District Court Judge Melville Gerry
players.role: Judge associated with Packer’s 1883 death sentence and its disputed wording
players.body: Judge M.B. Gerry sentenced Packer after the prosecution argued that Swan’s remains showed signs of a struggle while the others appeared to have been killed in their sleep. A local newspaper, quoting Larry Dolan, attributed a highly slangy condemnation to Gerry, including references to Democrats and a sentence to hang “dead, dead, dead.” Court records present the sentence in a conventional form. The Colorado Supreme Court later reversed the sentence in 1885 because the applicable law was ex post facto and officially upheld it in 1899.

players.name: David Bailey
players.role: Museum of Western Colorado curator who investigated a pistol fragment linked to Bell’s remains
players.body: In 1994, David P. Bailey found an 1862 Colt revolver while inventorying a historic firearms collection and investigated whether it supported Packer’s claim that he shot Shannon Bell. After a hole was found in Bell’s hip bone during the 1989 exhumation, Bailey suspected it was a bullet hole; the fragment’s chemical composition matched bullets from his Colt. Bailey believed the evidence supported Packer’s self-defense account, although Grant Houston and Michelle Pierce remained unconvinced. In mock trials, juries acquitted Packer more often when Bailey’s evidence was included.

players.name: James Starrs
players.role: Forensic-law professor who led the 1989 exhumation of Packer’s alleged victims
players.body: James E. Starrs, a George Washington University law professor specializing in forensic science, led the July 17, 1989, exhumation of the five bodies. Starrs and Walter H. Birkby said cannibalism could not be scientifically demonstrated, but Starrs concluded that the evidence was sufficient to find Packer had murdered his companions, probably for their belongings, and then resorted to cannibalism out of necessity. He later said he had proven Packer “guilty as sin.”

players.name: Los Pi
players.role: Variant name for the Los Piños Indian Agency, Packer’s 1874 destination
players.body: The supplied accounts use “Los Pi” in connection with the Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado. Packer and other prospectors planned to reach the agency before continuing toward Breckenridge. Packer arrived there alone on April 16, 1874, after 65 days, carrying a Winchester rifle, a skinning knife, and a coffee pot with live coals. The agency is where his distressed arrival, questioning, and competing accounts of the journey entered the historical record.

players.name: General Charles Adams
players.role: Officer who recorded Packer’s confession and took him for trial
players.body: General Charles Adams and his men helped Packer to a table after his arrival at the agency, where he ate so quickly that he vomited. Adams questioned him about the money and belongings he carried, recorded his confession, and had him sign it as a sworn statement. He later led Packer and others into the mountains to search for the bodies, without finding them, and confirmed Packer’s identity before taking him away for trial. Adams also obtained a later admission that Packer had only been a guide and did not know the mountain route.

players.name: Colorado State Penitentiary
players.role: Canon City prison where Packer was held before his 1901 parole
players.body: The Colorado State Penitentiary held Packer after his conviction, where he made horsehair bridles. Polly Pry visited him there in 1899 during her campaign for his release. After pressure from supporters and the Denver Post, the Colorado governor paroled Packer in 1901. The prison recurs as the setting for both his incarceration and the press effort that preceded his parole.

players.name: Los Pin
players.role: Variant name for the Los Piños Indian Agency, the prospectors’ planned outpost
players.body: The supplied accounts use “Los Pin” for the Los Piños Indian Agency in southwestern Colorado. The prospectors planned to travel there as the nearest outpost before going on to Breckenridge, and Packer and five others left for it on February 9. Packer eventually reached the agency alone, while two men from the river-route party arrived later. The name recurs in accounts of the expedition’s route, Packer’s arrival, and the differing reports of when he reached safety.

players.name: Frank Miller
players.role: Member of Packer’s group and alleged victim whose knife Packer possessed
players.body: Frank “Butcher” Miller was one of the five men traveling with Packer. Packer said Shannon Bell killed Miller while he slept, but also said the group later chose Miller as the next person to butcher because he was stocky and had soft flesh. Packer took Miller’s skinning knife, which Nutter noticed; Packer claimed Miller had left it stuck in a tree. Miller’s head was missing from the campsite, and his remains were heavily scavenged.

players.name: Gunnison River
players.role: River route followed by the prospectors’ alternate party toward the Los Piños agency
players.body: Chief Ouray recommended dropping to the Gunnison River and following it north to the agency. The party split, with five men following Oliver Loutsenhizer along the river while six, including Packer, entered the San Juan Mountains; Bob McGrue guided the river-route party until the horses could go no farther. Preston Nutter later reached the agency as leader of that group, and two of its men eventually arrived there. The river also appears in accounts of where Packer became lost and where evidence connected to Shannon Bell was later found.

players.name: James Humphrey
players.role: Member of Packer’s group and alleged victim in conflicting accounts of the deaths
players.body: James Humphrey was one of the five men traveling with Packer. Packer first said Shannon Bell killed Humphrey while he slept, and elsewhere said Humphrey was to be sacrificed after Miller; in an amended account, Packer said Humphrey died from exposure to extreme cold. Humphrey’s remains, like George Noon’s, were described as a largely flayed torso attached to skeletal legs, with head injuries suggesting a hatchet. His body was among the five exhumed by James Starrs in 1989.

players.name: United States
players.role: Country whose legal and historical records frame the Packer cannibalism case
players.body: The material describes Packer as one of four people historically convicted for cannibalism in the United States and calls the incident the only known U.S. trial associated with human cannibalism. It also notes that cannibalism itself is not illegal in the United States unless someone commits murder to obtain flesh. The case recurs through national reporting, including the United Press International account of Governor Richard Lamm’s refusal of a posthumous pardon, and through annual Packer events held in Colorado and twelve other states.

record.what: Alferd G. Packer was born in 1842 and died in 1907.
record.context: This is one of several biographical records that use different spellings for Packer’s name. Its lifespan differs from another record in the chronology, indicating that the surviving accounts are not fully consistent.

record.what: Alferd E. Packer lived from 1842 to 1909.
record.context: This record preserves a variant form of Packer’s name and a different reported year of death. The discrepancy matters because later entries rely on identifying the same historical figure across conflicting records.

record.what: Alfred Griner Packer was born on January 21, 1842, in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, U.S.
record.context: The precise birth date and Pennsylvania location provide the strongest identifying details among the birth records. They give the chronology a specific starting point for tracing his later military and western history.

record.what: Alferd Packer was born near Pittsburgh in 1842.
record.context: This version gives only a broad geographic origin rather than a precise birthplace. It is consistent with the Pennsylvania setting but less specific than the detailed birth record.

record.what: Rebecca A. Newman was born in 1846 in Herkimer, New York, and worked as a schoolteacher while living in the Bronx neighborhood of New York City.
record.context: This adds education-related work and a New York City connection to Newman’s background. Her employment as a teacher provides the main occupational detail attached to her in the chronology.

record.what: She was born to a wealthy family in 1857.
record.context: This detail adds family status to the subject’s background. Because it gives no name or location, it cannot by itself connect the subject to the other biographical entries.

record.what: In the 1950s, a rusted 1862 Colt Police Model .32 five-shot revolver was found on Cannibal Plateau with two shots missing.
record.context: The weapon provides a tangible object associated with the Cannibal Plateau episode. Its discovery location and missing ammunition make it suggestive evidence, but the entry does not identify its owner or explain how it came to be there.

record.what: Packer enlisted on April 22, 1862, in Winona, Minnesota, and was assigned to Company F of the 16th Infantry Regiment.
record.context: This marked the beginning of Packer’s recorded military service during the Civil War. His assignment to a specific infantry company established the regiment later associated with his veteran’s grave marker.

record.what: His grave has a veteran's tombstone listing his original regiment in 1862 because his original grave marker was stolen.
record.context: The surviving marker links Packer’s burial memory to his earliest recorded military service. The loss of the original marker means that the later monument became especially important evidence of how his service was commemorated.

record.what: Packer enlisted in the 8th Iowa Cavalry Regiment at Ottumwa, Iowa, on June 25, 1863.
record.context: This represents a subsequent enlistment in a cavalry regiment after his earlier infantry service. It shows that his military record involved more than one unit and enlistment period.

record.what: Packer was discharged again on April 22, 1864, because of epilepsy.
record.context: Epilepsy brought this period of military service to an end. The discharge provides a documented medical reason for his departure from the cavalry regiment.

record.what: Alferd Packer led a party of 21 prospectors that departed from Bingham Canyon, Utah, on November 8, 1873, hoping to be among the first to locate mining claims in the San Juan region.
record.context: The expedition placed Packer in a group pursuing the economic opportunities associated with the San Juan region. Its departure created the journey that later accounts connect with the winter crisis and cannibalism accusation.

record.what: The prospecting party entered the San Juan region in the winter of 1873-1874.
record.context: The party’s movement into the San Juan region brought the prospectors into the setting where the expedition’s difficulties unfolded. The winter timing is important because it places the journey under severe seasonal conditions.

record.what: In November 1873, Packer lied to five men and 15 other miners near Bingham Canyon, Utah Territory, telling them he could guide them to Colorado Territory’s rich precious metal region.
record.context: The expedition began through a claim that Packer could lead miners to valuable territory. That deception helps explain how the larger prospecting group was assembled and why he became central to its journey.

record.what: After joining the 1873 party, Alfred got the group as far as just outside Montrose by getting lucky.
record.context: Reaching the area outside Montrose kept the party moving toward southwestern Colorado despite the lack of a clearly established route. The account attributes this progress to chance rather than demonstrated guiding ability.

record.what: Several months earlier, Alfred had joined a party that left Bingham Canyon, Utah, on November 20, 1873, as part of a group of 20 men.
record.context: This is another account of the expedition’s formation, but it gives a different departure date and group size from other entries. The variation shows that the chronology preserves competing versions of how the journey began.

record.what: The men left by November 1873.
record.context: This compressed statement places the departure within the broad period when the expedition was organized. It offers little detail, but it supports the repeated chronology placing the journey in late 1873.

record.what: In the fall of 1873, Packer left on an expedition toward San Juan country with 20 prospectors.
record.context: This version emphasizes the expedition’s destination and the number of prospectors involved. It contributes to the recurring picture of Packer traveling west with a sizeable mining party before the winter crisis.

record.what: Alfred Packer was accused of cannibalism during the winter of 1873-1874.
record.context: The accusation tied Packer’s name to the expedition’s most notorious event. Its winter timing places the allegation within the same period as the party’s entry into the San Juan region.

record.what: In late 1873, Packer joined a group of 20 prospectors headed to southwestern Colorado.
record.context: Joining this prospecting group connected Packer directly to the route toward southwestern Colorado. The late-1873 timing aligns this account with the other descriptions of the expedition’s departure.

record.what: After the war, Packer traveled around the country and reached Utah in 1873.
record.context: His movements after the war eventually brought him into the region where the later investigation and controversy unfolded. This placed him in Utah before the events that made his name notorious.

record.what: In August 1874, a prospecting party discovered the bodies of the five missing men.
record.context: The discovery ended the uncertainty surrounding the missing party and supplied the physical basis for the case against Packer. It also made the winter expedition a matter of public investigation rather than rumor.

record.what: Packer appealed for a retrial on the grounds that the crime was committed on the Ute Reservation in early 1874 and should therefore have been subject to federal rather than local jurisdiction.
record.context: The appeal shifted attention from the deaths themselves to the authority of the court that handled the case. Packer’s lawyers argued that the location of the alleged crime could invalidate the local proceedings.

record.what: The party reached the Ute encampment near present-day Montrose on January 21, 1874, with their food and supplies exhausted.
record.context: By the time the group found refuge with the Utes, its ability to continue independently had nearly collapsed. The encounter explains why the party’s later decision to leave carried such serious risks.

record.what: Alferd G. Packer was the prospector accused of committing murder during the winter of early 1874.
record.context: Packer is the central figure connecting the expedition, the deaths, the confession, and the later legal proceedings. His identity as a prospector places him among the men drawn toward the newly discovered goldfields.

record.what: Packer and five others ventured into the wilderness of the San Juan Mountains in January 1874 against the advice of Chief Ouray.
record.context: The expedition began as a hazardous attempt to reach the goldfields, but it also involved disregarding the warning of an experienced Ute leader. That choice set the group on the course leading to its isolation in the mountains.

record.what: Those five men followed Packer into a storm on February 9, 1874.
record.context: The departure transformed an already difficult journey into a winter survival crisis. Once the men entered the storm, their chances depended on finding food and shelter in conditions that had already defeated the larger party.

record.what: Packer committed cannibalism during the winter of 1874 after guiding a group of five men into Colorado Territory’s San Juan Mountains during a snowstorm.
record.context: The allegation combines the expedition’s failed objective with the deaths that followed its entrapment. It became the defining charge in the story, linking Packer’s leadership to the group’s collapse.

record.what: In 1874, six men set off into Colorado's San Juan Mountains in the middle of winter to reach newly discovered goldfields on the other side.
record.context: The men were pursuing mineral wealth, not simply traveling through the mountains. Their decision to make the crossing in midwinter made the search for gold inseparable from the dangers of exposure, hunger, and isolation.

record.what: On the morning of April 16, 1874, workers at Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado were eating breakfast when a distressed man burst into the mess hall.
record.context: Packer’s sudden appearance interrupted the agency’s ordinary routine and immediately presented officials with an extraordinary account. His arrival began the process by which the missing party and the events in the mountains became known.

record.what: Packer became famous after confessing to eating his dead comrades while trapped in the San Juan Mountains in February 1874.
record.context: The confession gave the public a concrete explanation for the men’s disappearance and made Packer a widely recognized figure. It also ensured that the episode would be remembered primarily through the most shocking part of his account.

record.what: The 10th Grade, 8th Grade, and 4th Grade versions repeat that Packer was a prospector born in 1842 and tied to the February 1874 San Juan Mountains cannibalism story.
record.context: The repeated classroom versions preserve a simplified identification of Packer and the episode. Their consistency shows how the February 1874 story became the standard way of introducing him.

record.what: On February 9, 1874, Al Packer and five other prospectors left the Ute leader Ouray’s winter camp.
record.context: The men left a place of relative shelter and entered the mountains at the moment when the expedition became most dangerous. Their departure is the key turning point between seeking assistance and attempting the fatal crossing.

record.what: Cabazon had been one of the original members of the Utah mining party who stayed in Chief Ouray's camp in the winter of 1874.
record.context: Cabazon’s presence connects the mining party to the period when some members remained at Ouray’s camp. That connection helps distinguish the men who continued into the mountains from those who did not.

record.what: Packer's lawyers later discovered that the 1874 murder statutes had been repealed and replaced with a savings clause.
record.context: The defense found a statutory problem that could affect whether the prosecution remained legally valid. The issue added a technical avenue of attack to Packer’s effort to obtain a new trial.

record.what: Local hunters and officials said the winter of 1874 was one of the worst they had seen for some time, but the San Juans campsite still had abundant wildlife including deer and antelope.
record.context: The testimony presents the winter as exceptionally severe without proving that game was entirely absent. This complicates any explanation based only on starvation and leaves the group’s choices and circumstances central to the account.

record.what: On January 21, 1874, the party reached Chief Ouray’s encampment near Montrose, Colorado, in the Uncompahgre Valley.
record.context: The encampment became the party’s last substantial stopping point before the fatal departure. Its location in the Uncompahgre Valley also anchors the opening stage of the journey geographically.

record.what: On April 16, 1874, 65 days after departing, Packer emerged from the woods alone and crossed a frozen lake bed to the Los Pinós Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado.
record.context: His arrival after 65 days established both the length of his ordeal and the isolation of the missing men. Reaching the agency gave authorities their first direct link to what had happened in the mountains.

record.what: Packer confessed to cannibalism during the winter of 1874.
record.context: The admission made Packer’s own account the central evidence associated with the episode. It transformed an unexplained disappearance into a criminal and moral controversy.

record.what: Only Packer returned in the winter of 1874.
record.context: The fact that no one else returned made Packer the sole surviving witness to the expedition’s final days. That survival gave his account unusual importance while leaving the circumstances dependent on his version of events.

record.what: Packer gave three confessions: one in May 1874, one in March 1883, and a final confession in a letter to the Rocky Mountain News in August 1897.
record.context: The changing accounts left a record that could be compared against the prosecution’s case and later public arguments about Packer. His final statement appeared long after the original trial, keeping the story alive into the late nineteenth century.

record.what: Packer was a prospector who set out for Colorado’s gold fields with five other men in winter 1874.
record.context: The expedition placed Packer among a small group entering dangerous country at the height of the gold rush. Their decision created the circumstances from which his later isolation and notoriety emerged.

record.what: Starrs said that over the years since 1874 Packer had been lionized, apologized for, and sympathized with, and that people had tried to have him pardoned posthumously.
record.context: Packer’s reputation never settled into a single judgment. The competing efforts to condemn, excuse, or pardon him show how the case became a lasting public controversy rather than a closed criminal episode.

record.what: Packer was one of six prospectors who left for the Colorado mountains in February 1874 despite winter dangers because they were flush with gold fever.
record.context: Gold fever overrode the practical danger of traveling in the mountains during winter. That choice made the group vulnerable before the later violence and disappearance occurred.

record.what: Packer became the source of legend after he wandered out of the mountains alone in April 1874.
record.context: His solitary return transformed an obscure expedition into a mystery that attracted repeated explanations. The legend grew because the other prospectors did not emerge with him.

record.what: Colorado became a state in 1876, and before statehood Colorado Territory had no statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder.
record.context: The absence of a territorial murder statute created a legal obstacle to prosecuting the case at the time of the alleged killings. Statehood changed the legal setting in which the authorities could pursue the matter.

record.what: The Hinsdale County Courthouse in Lake City was built in 1877 and is the oldest operating courthouse in Colorado.
record.context: The courthouse supplied the physical setting for the later proceedings and connects the case to an institution that has continued operating. Its survival gives the story a tangible link to Colorado’s early legal history.

record.what: Packer was apprehended in Wyoming in 1883.
record.context: The Wyoming apprehension ended the long period during which Packer was away from Colorado authorities. It made possible the renewed investigation and prosecution that followed.

record.what: Packer was first found guilty of murder in 1883 in Lake City, but that conviction was overturned.
record.context: The initial verdict did not end the legal dispute, because the conviction was later set aside. That reversal opened the way for further proceedings and kept the case from concluding with the first judgment.

record.what: Packer escaped from jail and remained on the lam for nearly 10 years until March 1883, when he was found in Douglas, Wyoming, under the alias John Swartze.
record.context: The escape and years under an assumed name delayed accountability while allowing the case to become more mysterious. His eventual discovery brought the old mountain tragedy back into public and judicial view.

record.what: Packer said he was not arrested or censured by anyone until 1883 and that he was in the country and seen by all men during all the time.
record.context: Packer’s own account rejected the idea that he had been a fugitive or publicly condemned during the intervening years. This denial contrasts with the authorities’ later pursuit and the criminal case built against him.

record.what: In 1883, one of the original prospectors from the winter with Chief Ouray had opened a supply shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming.
record.context: The shopkeeper’s connection to the original expedition created an unexpected route by which Packer could be recognized. The episode shows how surviving links from the 1874 party helped expose his assumed identity.

record.what: On March 11, 1883, Packer was discovered in Cheyenne, Wyoming, by Jean 'Frenchy' Cabazon living under the alias 'John Schwartze'.
record.context: Recognition by someone connected to the earlier expedition broke through Packer’s alias. His discovery in Cheyenne converted a long-standing disappearance into an arrestable case.

record.what: After seven days of testimony and examinations, he was found guilty of the premeditated murder of Israel Swan and sentenced to death by hanging on May 19, 1883.
record.context: The trial treated the deaths as deliberate rather than merely the result of an expedition gone disastrously wrong. The death sentence marked the harshest possible legal response to the prosecution’s account.

record.what: In his 1883 confession, Packer said, “I went back to the fire covered the men up and fetched to the camp the piece of meat that was near the fire.”
record.context: This detail placed Packer at the camp after the deaths and showed him handling the remains and food. It became part of the evidence used to portray his conduct as deliberate survival at the victims’ expense.

record.what: In his 1883 confession, Packer said he tried to get away every day but could not and lived off the flesh of the men for the bigger part of the 60 days he was out.
record.context: The confession presented the ordeal as a prolonged struggle in which escape repeatedly failed. Its account of cannibalism supplied some of the most shocking material behind Packer’s enduring notoriety.

record.what: District Court Judge Melville Gerry reportedly said at sentencing in 1883, “stand up, Alferd Packer, you voracious, man-eating s– of a b—-.”
record.context: The reported outburst became one of the most famous expressions of the case’s moral condemnation. Its crude wording also helped turn the sentencing into part of Packer folklore.

record.what: Packer was found guilty of Bell’s murder in 1883.
record.context: This verdict identified Bell as the victim whose death supported the conviction at that stage of the proceedings. It also reflects the narrower legal finding within a case that involved accusations concerning all five companions.

record.what: Gerry’s actual statement ordered Alfred Packer confined in the jail of Hinsdale County until May 19, 1883.
record.context: The documented sentencing language was administrative and legal, not the notorious insult later attributed to Gerry. That distinction separates the surviving judicial order from the story’s more memorable folklore.

record.what: In 1883 Packer was charged with murdering all five companions.
record.context: The prosecution’s theory extended beyond a single death and treated the entire group’s disappearance as criminally connected. This broad charge framed the trial as an accounting for the fate of all five companions.

record.what: Packer’s trial began on April 9, 1883, and the courtroom was filled to capacity.
record.context: The capacity crowd indicates that the case had become a major public spectacle. The trial marked the beginning of the courtroom phase that would determine whether Packer’s account could withstand formal scrutiny.

record.what: In October 1885, the Colorado Supreme Court reversed the sentence as based on an ex post facto law.
record.context: The ruling did not necessarily resolve the underlying accusations; it invalidated the legal basis for the sentence. By applying the ex post facto principle, the court forced the case back into the trial process.

record.what: Packer’s death sentence was overturned by the Colorado Supreme Court in 1885 because of a “grandfather clause.”
record.context: This account emphasizes a procedural defect rather than a finding that Packer was innocent. The defective legal provision made the original death sentence unsustainable.

record.what: After a second trial in 1885, Packer received a 40-year sentence.
record.context: The new proceeding replaced the death penalty with a fixed prison term. That result kept Packer in custody while substantially reducing the severity of the punishment.

record.what: Packer's retrial in 1886 found him guilty of five counts of manslaughter.
record.context: The verdict narrowed the legal outcome into five separate manslaughter findings. It also shows that the retrial continued to hold Packer responsible for the deaths, though not under a murder conviction.

record.what: Packer was eventually convicted of manslaughter in a second trial in Gunnison in 1886.
record.context: This conviction confirmed that the retrial did not end in acquittal. Its location in Gunnison connects the renewed prosecution to the place associated with the original case.

record.what: Packer was resentenced in 1886 to 40 years in prison.
record.context: The resentencing established the term that governed Packer’s imprisonment after the retrial. It transformed the unsettled consequences of the reversed sentence into a definite period of incarceration.

record.what: In 1887, Adams relented and forwarded Newman’s letter to the State Penitentiary.
record.context: Adams’s decision allowed Newman’s appeal to reach prison officials after being withheld. The forwarded letter became part of the later effort to influence Packer’s treatment and prospects for release.

record.what: In 1898, Frederick Bonfils hired her for The Denver Post.
record.context: The hiring gave her a professional newspaper platform from which she could pursue prominent stories. That position helps explain her later involvement in coverage connected with Packer.

record.what: In 1899, Denver Post writer Polly Pry visited Packer at the Colorado State Penitentiary in Canon City.
record.context: The prison visit brought the imprisoned Packer directly into the newspaper’s narrative. It supplied the reporter with personal access for an article that could shape public sympathy or controversy.

record.what: The retrial eventually led to a pardon for Packer on January 7, 1901.
record.context: The conclusion of the retrial process opened the way for executive relief rather than continued imprisonment under the existing sentence. The account presents the pardon as the eventual result of sustained efforts on Packer’s behalf.

record.what: After enough pressure, the Colorado governor paroled Alfred in 1901.
record.context: The release followed organized public pressure rather than occurring quietly or automatically. That pressure made Packer’s imprisonment a matter of political intervention.

record.what: He was paroled on February 8, 1901, after a campaign led first by his old acquaintance Duane Hatch.
record.context: Hatch’s role shows that the campaign began with someone who already knew Packer. The later parole therefore emerged from personal advocacy that developed into a broader effort.

record.what: Former Gov. Charles Thomas paroled Packer in 1901.
record.context: A former governor’s involvement gave the request political weight. His action indicates that support for Packer extended beyond private acquaintances and newspaper advocates.

record.what: Packer was paroled in 1901 after a Denver Post columnist crusaded on his behalf.
record.context: The columnist’s crusade made the case a recurring public argument rather than a single news report. Newspaper advocacy helped sustain attention until the authorities granted relief.

record.what: She met Alfred Packer in 1901 while writing an article about the prison where he was incarcerated.
record.context: The meeting gave her firsthand material for writing about the prisoner and the institution holding him. It also connected her later advocacy or coverage to direct personal contact.

record.what: Packer received parole in 1905.
record.context: This later release claim conflicts with the accounts placing Packer’s parole earlier. It should therefore be read as a separate or competing version of the chronology rather than an uncomplicated continuation.

record.what: Alfred Packer died alone in 1907 in Littleton, Colorado, at age 69.
record.context: His death brought the long sequence of prosecution, imprisonment, and release to an end. Dying alone emphasizes the isolation that remained after the public controversy had passed.

record.what: Alfred died in 1907 at age 65.
record.context: The age given here differs from the other supplied accounts. The shared point is that his death closed the life story after the legal controversy and imprisonment.

record.what: Alferd Packer died in 1907.
record.context: This entry confirms the endpoint of Packer’s life without resolving the conflicting age reports. Its brevity leaves the surrounding circumstances to the fuller death accounts.

record.what: The lower-grade versions repeat that he made horsehair bridles and elaborate Victorian dollhouses in prison and died in 1907.
record.context: These accounts add colorful details about Packer’s prison years and final period, but their explicitly low-grade status makes them unreliable as firm biographical evidence. They belong to the later tradition surrounding him rather than to a securely documented account.

record.what: Alfred Griner Packer died on April 23, 1907, in Jefferson County, Colorado, U.S., at age 65.
record.context: This supplies a precise death date and location for the chronology, fixing the end of Packer’s life in Colorado. The age also provides a point of comparison with the less precise or duplicated death notices that follow.

record.what: Packer died in 1907 in Jefferson County, Colorado, and the official cause of death listed was "Senility -- trouble and worry."
record.context: The wording of the official cause gives the death record an unusually subjective character, emphasizing decline and emotional strain rather than a specific disease. It also shows how Packer’s final years were documented in bureaucratic language.

record.what: Packer died in 1907 at age 65.
record.context: This shorter notice confirms the age given in the more detailed death records. Its lack of a date or location makes it supplementary rather than the chronology’s principal record of his death.

record.what: Rebecca A. Newman died in 1926 at age 80.
record.context: The supplied material gives Newman a later endpoint but no further role or connection in the surrounding story. Her entry therefore serves as a biographical marker rather than an event that changes the Packer narrative.

record.what: Leonel Campbell Ross O'Bryan was born in 1857 and died on July 16, 1938, aged 80.
record.context: The full name and exact age provide a formal identification for the person whose death is recorded again under the name Polly Pry. The matching date and age make the two notices part of the same biographical thread.

record.what: Polly Pry died on 16 July 1938 at the age of eighty.
record.context: This notice preserves the public or familiar name associated with the death recorded under O’Bryan’s fuller name. Its repetition of the date and age reinforces the identification across differently styled records.

record.what: Phil Ochs, the songwriter behind Packer’s ballad, wrote The Ballad of Alferd Packer in 1964 about the expedition and its aftermath.
record.context: Ochs’s song carried the expedition and its aftermath into popular culture decades after the events. It helped turn the episode from a historical crime story into a subject for later reinterpretation and remembrance.

record.what: The Arrow reported in January 1965 that a blizzard caught the six men without sufficient food and that Packer wandered into the Los Pinos Agency in Southwest Colorado three months later.
record.context: The report offers a compressed narrative of the expedition’s crisis, emphasizing exposure, inadequate provisions, and Packer’s eventual reappearance. Its publication shows that the episode continued to circulate as a dramatic news and historical subject.

record.what: In 1968 students at the University of Colorado in Boulder renamed the student union restaurant the Alferd E. Packer Memorial Grill.
record.context: The renaming transformed Packer from a condemned historical figure into a source of campus humor and institutional identity. It also established a public memorial that later accounts continued to mention.

record.what: The lower-grade versions repeat that Lake City still promotes Packer-related attractions and that the University of Colorado renamed its restaurant after him in 1968.
record.context: These low-grade accounts connect two parts of Packer’s modern legacy: tourism around Lake City and the university’s commemorative restaurant name. Their limited reliability matters because they describe persistence of the legend rather than newly documented events.

record.what: In 1968, students at the University of Colorado Boulder named their new cafeteria grill the Alferd G. Packer Memorial Grill.
record.context: The cafeteria name made Packer’s notoriety part of everyday student life at the university. In doing so, it recast a violent episode as an irreverent piece of campus culture.

record.what: The Littleton Cemetery Association cemented over Packer's grave in 1973 to deter grave robbing and vandalism.
record.context: Sealing the grave shows that Packer’s notoriety had practical consequences long after his death. The measure treated vandalism and grave robbing as continuing risks and altered the physical site of his burial.

record.what: The song appeared on several compilations after Ochs's death in 1976, including the 2010 On My Way compilation of demos from 1963.
record.context: Ochs’s death did not end the song’s circulation; later compilations continued to preserve and distribute it. The 2010 release also reached back to early demo material, extending the song’s documentary and cultural afterlife.

record.what: In 1977, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Bob Bergland tried to terminate a contract for the department's cafeteria food service but was blocked by the General Services Administration.
record.context: The failed effort to end the cafeteria contract created the bureaucratic dispute that made a symbolic response possible. It placed the Packer name within a confrontation over federal food-service administration.

record.what: To embarrass the GSA, Bergland and his employees held a press conference on August 10, 1977, to unveil a plaque naming the executive cafeteria The Alferd Packer Memorial Grill.
record.context: The plaque was deliberately used as a public embarrassment directed at the GSA, not simply as a memorial. That episode broadened Packer’s image into a political and workplace joke, giving the name another layer of public meaning.

record.what: An almost completely fictitious biopic of Packer’s exploits, The Legend of Alfred Packer, was released in 1980.
record.context: The film helped popularize Packer’s story while openly departing from reliable history. Its fictionalization shows how the legend could be reshaped for entertainment rather than preserved as a factual account.

record.what: The United Press International reported in 1982 that then-Gov. Richard Lamm had declined Packer’s posthumous pardon the year before.
record.context: The pardon controversy brought Packer’s case back into official public discussion nearly a century after the expedition. Lamm’s refusal kept the question of guilt and justification unresolved in the state’s modern memory.

record.what: At a bust unveiling of Packer at the Capitol Rotunda in 1982, Lamm said, “I realize that several of you have a bone to pick with me because of my refusal to grant Alferd Packer an unconditional pardon last year.”
record.context: Lamm’s remark acknowledged that the ceremony was also a venue for criticism of his earlier decision. The bust therefore commemorated Packer while simultaneously highlighting the unresolved dispute over whether he deserved formal forgiveness.

record.what: At the 1982 bust unveiling, Lamm said, “you claim that the evidence indicates that Mr. Packer killed but one man, and that one only in self-defense.”
record.context: The statement presents the defense’s central argument: that the evidence supported only one killing and that it was self-defense. By placing that claim in the pardon debate, it shows how competing interpretations of the episode remained politically and publicly active.

record.what: At the 1982 bust unveiling, Lamm said, “Unfortunately, the proof was in the pudding and Alferd ate that, too.”
record.context: Lamm’s remark used gallows humor to connect Packer’s alleged crime with the ceremony honoring him. It also showed how the story could be treated simultaneously as local history and macabre entertainment.

record.what: The New York Times reported in 1982 that Lamm congratulated sculptor Tom Miller at Packer’s bust unveiling.
record.context: The newspaper account placed the unveiling within wider public attention rather than treating it as a purely local occasion. Lamm’s congratulations also associated the monument with the sculptor’s work.

record.what: The plaque also serves as a memorial to Stanley Weston, who worked at the USDA and died in 1984.
record.context: The memorial’s meaning extends beyond Packer himself, preserving the memory of a USDA worker connected to the story’s later history. Weston’s death also marks a point at which the plaque became a record of people involved in documenting Packer.

record.what: On July 17, 1989, James E. Starrs led an exhumation of the five bodies 115 years after Packer supposedly consumed his companions.
record.context: The exhumation transformed a nineteenth-century accusation into a modern forensic investigation. Recovering the remains created the possibility of testing the long-standing account against physical evidence.

record.what: The library holdings mentioned include books about Packer, including The Alfred G. Packer Victims Exhumation Project Lake City, Colorado, July 17, 1989.
record.context: These holdings preserve not only general accounts of Packer but also a record of the exhumation project itself. They show how the investigation became part of the documentary history surrounding the case.

record.what: On July 17, 1989, grad students excavated skeletons in Lake City, Colorado, as reporters and onlookers gathered around the dig.
record.context: The presence of reporters and spectators made the excavation a public event as well as a scientific undertaking. The scene linked contemporary media interest with the continuing fascination of the old disappearance.

record.what: In 1989, James Starrs concluded his investigation by calling Packer “guilty as sin.”
record.context: Starrs’s conclusion gave the investigation a blunt public verdict, even though the exhumation and testing had begun as an effort to examine the evidence. His phrasing helped fix the inquiry in popular memory as a judgment on Packer’s guilt.

record.what: Bailey discovered that a hole about the size of a thimble had been found in Bell’s hip bone during the 1989 exhumation.
record.context: The tiny opening in Bell’s bone supplied a potentially important clue about the manner of his death. By itself, however, the finding called for interpretation and further examination rather than resolving the entire case.

record.what: The Hinsdale County Historical Society shared the 1989 forensic samples with Richard Dujay, director of the Electron Microscopy Lab at Mesa State College.
record.context: Sharing the samples moved the evidence from local historical custody into specialized laboratory analysis. It created a bridge between the exhumation and later attempts to extract information with modern instruments.

record.what: CU film students Matt Stone, a CU film student involved in Packer’s retelling, and Trey Parker, a CU film student involved in Packer’s retelling, produced Cannibal! The Musical in 1993.
record.context: The project brought Packer’s story into the work of two CU film students who would become associated with its comic retelling. Their involvement helped shift the legend from historical subject to cult entertainment.

record.what: A more comedic and heavily fabricated film about him, Cannibal! The Musical, was released in 1993.
record.context: The film deliberately treated the material as comedy rather than as a straightforward reconstruction. Its fabricated elements demonstrate how far Packer’s public image had moved from documentary history toward folklore and parody.

record.what: The comedy musical Cannibal! The Musical was released exclusively to Boulder, Colorado, in 1993 and to the rest of the United States in 1996.
record.context: The limited initial release made the film’s circulation gradual rather than nationwide from the outset. Its later expansion allowed the Colorado story to reach a much broader audience.

record.what: In 1994, an 1862 Colt revolver was found at the murder site.
record.context: The discovery introduced a tangible object that might bear on Packer’s account of the killings. It therefore reopened interest in whether the surviving historical record could be connected to a specific weapon.

record.what: In 1994, David P. Bailey, Curator of History at the Museum of Western Colorado, investigated Packer's claim that he shot Bell.
record.context: Bailey’s work focused on testing one of the central physical claims in Packer’s story. The investigation tied the newly noticed firearm to the question of whether Bell had been shot as Packer said.

record.what: In 1994, David Bailey found an 1862 Colt revolver while inventorying a historic firearms collection.
record.context: Finding the revolver during an inventory gave the investigation an unexpected lead rather than a weapon with an established crime-scene history. Its significance depended on determining whether it could be connected to Packer.

record.what: In 1998 author James E. Bank wrote Alferd Packer’s Wilderness Cookbook.
record.context: The book carried the legend into a deliberately domestic and culinary form, turning the wilderness story into a themed work of popular culture. It reflects the continuing ability of Packer’s notoriety to generate inventive reinterpretations.

record.what: By 2000, Bailey had not yet proven a link between the antique pistol and Alfred Packer.
record.context: The absence of proof kept the revolver from becoming decisive evidence in the case. The weapon remained suggestive, but its connection to Packer was still unestablished.

record.what: In 2001, Dr. Richard Dujay at Mesa State College examined archived forensic samples from the 1989 exhumation with an electron microscope.
record.context: Dujay’s examination revisited material collected during the earlier exhumation with technology suited to very small or damaged traces. This extended the investigation beyond the original excavation and kept the physical evidence open to renewed analysis.

record.what: As of 2008, the skull was reported to be at Ripley's Museum in San Antonio, Texas, after being moved from New Orleans in the wake of Hurricane Katrina.
record.context: The skull’s reported movement illustrates how the physical remains became museum objects whose whereabouts could change over time. Hurricane Katrina further complicated the chain of custody and the public’s ability to locate it.

files.title: The bodies and escape
files.body:
When summer came, General Charles Adams led Alfred Packer and some men back into the mountains to search for and retrieve the bodies, but they found nothing. In August, while Alfred was awaiting trial for manslaughter, illustrator John Randolph crossed the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to the place where Alfred had said he left Shannon Bell, Randolph saw something sticking out of the ground. He smelled a terrible stench and found five men in different states of decomposition. One body was little more than bones, apparently after animals had gotten to it. Two bodies had blunt-force injuries to the head, and Shannon Bell’s body had been stripped to the bones except for the hands and feet and also showed blunt-force trauma to the head. The remains suggested deliberate removal of edible portions rather than animal scavenging, except perhaps in the case of the first body. Randolph sketched the scene and reported it to authorities in Lake City, and a team of 20 volunteers later recovered the bodies. Harper’s Weekly covered the discovery in its October 17, 1874, edition and included Randolph’s illustration; the magazine’s visual treatment helped rivet national attention on the crime.

Other accounts identify him as John A. Randolph, an illustrator for Harper’s Weekly, and place the discovery the following August at the foot of Slumgullion Pass, two miles southeast of Lake City, Colorado, in a pine-shaded gulch above the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River. That place is now colloquially called Dead Man’s Gulch, or Deadman’s Gulch, and the site was five miles beyond town according to another account. The location matched Packer’s original claim that only Bell had been killed there. The snow covering the bodies and campsite had melted during the intervening four months. Randolph sketched the scene and alerted nearby Lake City authorities. The local coroner and law enforcement then went to the site with about 20 volunteers and found all five missing men in various states of decomposition, after four months exposed to the elements and animals. First responders said it appeared that “extreme violence” had befallen them. Frank Miller’s head was missing from the campsite; Miller’s and Israel Swan’s corpses had been heavily scavenged and were little more than scattered bones, and Swan’s skull had a jagged chunk missing. George Noon and James Humphrey were largely flayed torsos of rotting viscera attached to skeletal legs, though their faces remained intact and bearded; Humphrey’s face was slightly more decayed than Noon’s. Noon and Humphrey had received blows to the head that suggested a hatchet, and their bodies had noticeable broken bones. Bell lay with skeletal legs splayed and his arms at his sides. His arms had been crudely cut to the bones while his hands were still fully skinned, and his remaining corpse was a mass of viscera inside an almost wholly flayed torso. His face still had a thick red beard and bushy hair. The lack of noticeable decay in Bell’s face suggested that he was the last to die, and the top of his skull had been ripped open.

The coroner concluded that the men had been killed by blows to the head while they slept. None of the bodies had defensive wounds, and all had similar skull marks. The three bodies that were still intact or partly intact had flesh and muscle cut from choice, meaty locations, but no attempt had been made to consume bone marrow or organs. The men had rags or tattered cloths tied under their rotting feet in place of shoes, suggesting that they had eaten the leather from their footwear after running out of other food. Moldy and tattered blankets lay beneath and beside the bodies. A beaten path led from the corpses to a crude, makeshift shelter used by Packer. Evidence suggested that the deaths occurred before the supplies were totally exhausted, and inside the shelter investigators found possessions belonging to the men that Packer had left behind. Preston Nutter accompanied the party to the site and identified the remains as the five missing men. A rifle broken in two was found nearby; because of the damage on the remains, it was presumed to have been used to bludgeon one or more of the men. Officials buried the remains at the site, then returned to Packer’s makeshift jail to confront him, but he was missing.

The condition and location of the remains contradicted Packer’s version of events. The bodies were all together in one place rather than scattered across miles, and Humphrey and Noon still had large portions of flesh, muscle, and organs that could have been eaten before Bell allegedly tried to murder Packer. The theory at the time was that Packer killed the men for their possessions before supplies ran out, became trapped by snow and weather, and lived for months in his makeshift shelter, walking to the bodies and slicing off meat as he needed it. The area northeast of Lake City where Packer’s party got lost is labeled “Cannibal Plateau” on maps, while the site where the bodies were found is called “Deadman’s Gulch” or “Dead Man’s Gulch”; the lower-grade versions likewise repeat that these names are associated with the case.

The jail was little more than a log cabin on ranch property belonging to the Saguache County sheriff. Months had passed with no definite evidence of a crime, no bodies discovered, and no formal charges against Packer other than the attempt on Herman Lauter’s life. Saguache County authorities were reportedly unhappy about taxpayer money being spent on housing and guarding him. Packer allegedly received a makeshift key for his irons, a penknife, and some food, and escaped easily. Another account says that, before his charge could be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, someone gave him a key, penknife, and food so he could escape. It was never established who helped him; Packer never said who assisted him, how it happened, or why, and it was presumed that his guard had been bribed by Packer or by someone else. He slipped out of his cell and was not seen again for nine years. The accounts variously say he remained on the run for eight years or nearly a decade, but agree that he escaped from the Saguache jail, changed his identity, and was eventually arrested in Wyoming before being returned to Hinsdale County or Lake City for trial. One account says he was living under the alias John Swartze when he was discovered in Douglas, Wyoming, in March 1883.

The generally accepted theory at the time was that Packer had joined the party by overstating his qualifications as a mountain guide familiar with the area and had, at best, led the men to miserable deaths through gross incompetence. A more popular theory said that he had set out from Ouray’s camp with the five men in a premeditated plan to lead them into the wilderness, kill them, and rob them. Nutter and Loutsenhizer tried to discredit Packer’s claimed qualifications as a guide and highlighted his character flaws, multiple stories, and inconsistencies. Local newspapers gave the case constant coverage, with sensational headlines, negative comments about Packer’s character, and imaginative theories that drew national and international attention. Nearly the entire population of Saguache, and soon nearly the entire country and beyond, regarded Packer’s culpability for the men’s deaths as beyond doubt. Cannibalism was not seen as the main issue in his guilt: people already knew the Donner Party story and could understand the need to eat in the wilderness to some degree.

Packer’s later account to General Adams was that he had been gone most of the day searching for food and returned in the late evening. He said he found Bell sitting near the fire roasting a piece of meat cut from Miller’s leg; Miller’s body lay furthest from the fire, down the stream, and his skull had been crushed with the hatchet. Packer said the other three men were lying near the fire with cuts to their foreheads from the hatchet, some having two or three cuts. He said Bell came at him with the hatchet, so he shot Bell, dropped his revolver in deep snow, and lost it. He built a crude shelter from stray logs to fight the snow and wind, then hunkered down for hours when another storm set in. Starving, he decided he had to eat something or die. He said he returned to the fire, covered the men, carried the piece of meat near the fire back to camp, cooked it, and ate it. He tried every day to get away but could not, so he lived off the men’s flesh for most of 60 days. There was also a report that a deer carcass had been found near the campsite, which damaged his claim that wildlife was so scarce that the men quickly had to resort to cannibalism.

The second hearing emphasized that winter travel through the San Juan Mountains was practically suicidal: snow could exceed six feet in a single downfall, while winds and temperatures were severe. Locals had given Packer a safe route beside a main water source that could have provided fresh fish and kept the party on course. Instead, he chose a mountain path with minimal supplies because he believed it would be faster. In fact, the route taken by Packer and his companions was nearly the same length as the recommended route, though less traversable and far more dangerous.

Later investigations left the evidence disputed. James E. Starrs, a professor of law specializing in forensic science at George Washington University, led an exhaustive search and, on July 17, 1989, found the remains near the Lake Fork River upstream from Lake City. The men had been buried only 13 inches below ground at the end of the residential driveway of a home belonging to a local surgeon. Starrs and Walter H. Birkby, a University of Arizona forensic anthropologist who assisted him, said cannibalism could never be scientifically demonstrated because proof would require a picture of the person actually eating human flesh. Packer never denied cannibalism, so it was not the investigation’s main purpose. Starrs nevertheless concluded that Packer had more than likely murdered his companions for their belongings and resorted to cannibalism out of necessity rather than intent. The men were reinterred with proper burial and funeral rites.

The exhumation showed apparent blunt-force trauma to the skulls of two men, with no other noteworthy disturbance apart from butchering. All skulls had damage to varying extents on their upper craniums, and fabric fibers inside some skulls suggested that the men’s heads may have been covered by a blanket at death. The three other skeletons showed defensive hacking marks across the radius and ulna bones of their forearms, including Bell’s skeleton; such marks could have been sustained while shielding the face and body from an attack. Packer claimed Bell had killed the others with hatchet blows to the head, but in his second version he never claimed that he had fought Bell off with the hatchet. All five skeletons had post-mortem injuries, including depressed fractures, butterfly fractures, butchering trauma, and hacking trauma, injuries that seemed to contradict Packer’s claim of minimal cannibalism. Two skeletons other than Bell’s had cylindrical puncture wounds in the pelvic bone. Some investigators have questioned whether the three pelvic marks were bear-scavenging marks or bullet wounds, and no definitive conclusion has been made. One proposed but explicitly plausible scenario is that Packer bludgeoned two men in their sleep, then shot the three remaining men in the hips to incapacitate them; they fought him while he wielded a hatchet, and he killed them with blows to the head before butchering them and using their flesh during the snowbound period and his journey. The differing decomposition states contradict that scenario. It would seem unlikely that Packer shot three of the five in the hip unless he meant to debilitate them before killing them, and further analysis of entry and exit geometry that might clarify the initial cause of death has not been done. Packer’s ultimate motive has therefore remained heavily debated, with several possible theories.

A different report of Starrs’s project said that he described Packer as having “butchered his five fellow prospectors to death and then skinned them for all their bones were worth.” Starrs led a team that exhumed the five victims from a mass grave in the San Juan Mountains the previous July and said the added scientific evidence convicted Packer “beyond any shadow of a doubt,” in his opinion. At a reporters’ gathering, he wore a T-shirt showing five skulls and crossed bones with the legend “Gimme Five! The Packer Project.” That account says Starrs reported that none of the victims had been shot, that four had been killed by hatchet blows to the head, and that the fifth skull had not been found. He said all five sets of bones showed numerous knife marks indicating defleshing, cited “unmistakable proof of cannibalism,” and said Packer used the Colorado winter as a “natural refrigerator,” eating human-flesh filets “morning, noon and night.” Starrs believed the initial motive was to steal the companions’ belongings and that Packer then turned to cannibalism. His stated aim was to settle the debate over Packer’s guilt and “put forensic science on parade.” The project cost an estimated $10,000 to $15,000 and used ground-penetrating radar and laboratory inspection of the remains. It did not settle the spelling of Packer’s first name: Starrs and official court papers used “Alfred,” while Packer signed his name “Alferd.” The first skull uncovered had a gaping hole in its forehead, prompting the sensational report “Professor Exhumes 100-Year-Old Victims of Colorado Cannibal.”

Birkby was less conclusive, saying the evidence neither corroborated nor refuted anything Packer said and that no solid physical evidence would ever show who committed the murders. Lake City’s former town clerk Michelle Pierce, an archival researcher who questioned Packer’s guilt, believes Packer did not murder the five men; her archival research found many details that do not match the official narrative, and she portrays Packer as a pitiable figure whose social problems stemmed from a misunderstood disease and the harsh judgments of contemporaries. Pierce says people disliked Packer largely because they were afraid of him. Grant Houston remained skeptical of the later gun evidence as well.

The Audrey Thrailkill firearms collection at the museum included a Colt revolver reportedly found at the crime site. David P. Bailey’s investigation into the pistol’s background found trial-era documents, including a Civil War veteran’s statement that Bell had been shot twice and the other victims killed with a hatchet. The veteran observed a severe bullet wound in Bell’s pelvic area and a bullet hole through Bell’s wallet. The gun’s accession card said it had been found where Alferd Packer killed and ate his companions. Three .38-caliber cartridges were still loaded in the revolver. Starrs had attributed a hole in Bell’s hip bone to scavenging animal fangs, but Bailey suspected a bullet. Dujay and his team found a tiny fragment of lead in samples from beneath Bell’s remains; spectrographic and chemical analysis matched it to bullets remaining in Bailey’s Colt revolver. Using a similar 1860s pistol, the team fired a bullet into an elk hip bone, and the resulting hole matched the one in Bell’s hip. Bailey believed this supported Packer’s claim that he shot Bell, and it appears certain that at least Bell was shot, but whether he was shot in self-defense remains unanswered. Houston said people had long found old guns and bullets near the massacre site and claimed they belonged to Packer or the prospectors, while Pierce was also unconvinced that Bailey’s pistol was the smoking gun.

The account says that Packer’s life was constantly threatened by nearby townspeople. It also states that no definitive conclusions have been made about the discoveries, including the proposed reconstruction of the killings. Mazzula’s book, *Al Packer, A Colorado Cannibal*, uses archaeology to investigate what happened during the ill-fated journey.

files.title: The trial and verdict
files.body:
At trial, several parts of Alfred Packer’s story were challenged. People believed the events had been deliberate and premeditated, and it was thought that Alfred had intentionally led the men astray in order to steal their possessions by any means necessary. The prosecution argued that Alfred’s survival story was an attempt to cover up the crime and called many witnesses to support that view. Some witnesses were from the original Utah party. Preston testified that Alfred was always trying to find out how much money the men had, or, as another account puts it, that he had been skulking around trying to learn how much money each man carried. Other witnesses testified about Alfred’s behavior after he reached Saguache and the conflicting stories he told. Otto Mears testified that Alfred had valuable Wells Fargo drafts when he emerged from the mountains, while Constable Herman Lauter testified that Alfred lunged at him with murder in his eyes when ordered to surrender a knife. The prosecution called Otto Mears, Larry Dolan, Oliver D. Loutsenhizer, and Preston Nutter; Preston Nutter served as the prosecution’s key witness. One account says the prosecution called about two dozen witnesses, while the trial narrative says it brought in witness after witness.

The sources give different dates for the opening of the first trial: one says that a trial began in Lake City on April 6, while another dates the beginning to April 9, 1883. Alfred pleaded not guilty. It was presumed that Israel Swan died on or around March 1, and the prosecution said in court that Swan’s remains showed signs of a struggle at death while the others appeared to have been killed in their sleep. When Alfred testified, he spoke for six hours, or, in another account, for more than six hours in a rambling manner. He admitted eating the other party members but swore that he only killed Shannon and that Shannon was responsible for everything else. The jury rejected Alfred’s story and found him guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges.
