Research Briefing

The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

11 sources27,100 raw words readquotes verified 100%2026-08-30
Corpus balance — dates: 2003-2026 · stance: believer (2), neutral (9)
SECTION 1

The Read

The most damaging evidence against Alferd Packer is not that he ate the men. He admitted that. It is that the bodies did not fit his explanation—and that, more than a century later, forensic investigators still disagreed about what those bones could prove. The eleven supplied entries are not eleven independent reconstructions: one is an archive catalogue rather than a narrative, while the long Colorado Encyclopedia entry appears four times at different reading levels. The remaining accounts largely repeat the public record: six prospectors entered the winter mountains, five died, Packer emerged alone, admitted cannibalism while denying murder, escaped, was convicted, and was later paroled after Polly Pry campaigned for him. No account offers a wholly separate eyewitness reconstruction of the killings. The strongest primary material is the surviving paper trail—Packer’s confessions and letters, court files, parole records, and Supreme Court case files—held with penitentiary and military records by the Colorado State Archives, alongside later examination of the remains. Packer’s reckless promise set the expedition on course. In late 1873, he joined roughly twenty gold seekers traveling from Utah toward Colorado’s goldfields after claiming he knew the route. People who knew him described him as argumentative, dishonest, greedy, lazy, and prone to getting lost; he had worked briefly as a guide, but not well. The party struggled through snow, lost the trail, exhausted its provisions, and resorted to horse feed. At Chief Ouray’s camp near Montrose, the starving prospectors received food and shelter, and Ouray warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing in such weather. He offered to let them remain through winter and gave the departing men provisions and directions toward the Los Pinos Agency by way of the Gunnison River. Packer argued instead for the direct mountain route. Five men followed him: Israel Swan, George Noon, Frank Miller, James Humphrey, and Shannon Wilson Bell. They left on February 9, 1874, with food for roughly two weeks, inadequate clothing, almost no matches, no snowshoes, and only a few firearms and tools. Packer reached the agency alone on April 16, after 65 days in the mountains. He arrived in rags, with cloth around his feet, a rifle, a knife, a coffee pot, and a beard, but did not look starved. Although he vomited when first fed, he soon drank whiskey, traveled to Saguache, spent over $100 at Dolan’s saloon on gambling and liquor, bought a $70 horse, spent another $78 at a general store, and made further purchases. Penniless when he joined the expedition, he now carried cash—apparently in different wallets—and possessed a missing man’s rifle and Frank Miller’s knife. Packer first said the others had abandoned him while he warmed frozen feet and that he survived on roots, rosebuds, rabbits, and moccasin leather. The surviving prospectors rejected this: the men would not have abandoned their guide, and the rifle and possessions made his account implausible. When Ute hunters brought human flesh found near the agency, Packer panicked and offered a sworn confession transcribed by clerk Herman Lauter. He said the men had first eaten those who died from hunger or exposure, that Bell killed some of the others, and that Packer killed Bell in self-defense before living on the bodies for nearly sixty days. Packer gave three principal confessions—May 1874, March 1883, and a 1897 letter—and varied the sequence. In one version, Swan and Humphrey died naturally, Miller was killed while Packer gathered wood, Bell shot Noon, and Packer shot Bell. In another, Bell killed the entire camp while Packer scouted, then attacked him with a hatchet. In his later account, Bell was roasting Miller’s flesh when Packer returned, charged him, and was shot and finished with a hatchet. The evidence suggested that Packer killed the men before absolute starvation, then returned to their bodies; cannibalism itself did not prove murder. In August, illustrator John A. Randolph of Harper’s Weekly, an illustrator for Harper’s Weekly, discovered all five bodies together in a pine-shaded gulch near the Lake Fork of the Gunnison, later called Dead Man’s Gulch. Finding them in one place contradicted Packer’s claim that they died separately and were left in different places. The remains showed severe violence: blows fractured skulls, Miller’s head was missing, and flesh had been removed in ways that appeared to exceed animal scavenging. Cloth tied around the feet suggested the men had eaten their shoes, and a path connected the bodies to a crude shelter where Packer had apparently stayed. A broken rifle lay nearby. People therefore developed a stark theory: Packer killed the men for their possessions before supplies were gone, became trapped by snow, and returned to the bodies for meat. The prosecution used the same logic. Hunters testified that deer, antelope, rabbits, and other game remained even in severe winter. Packer’s decision to abandon Ouray’s safer route looked, at minimum, grossly negligent and, at worst, deliberate. The case was that killings preceded absolute starvation, while Packer’s changing accounts and possession of money made robbery a motive. The evidence supports a narrower conclusion than either camp prefers: Bell was probably shot, Packer probably ate the bodies, and deliberate violence is plausible without every part of the prosecution’s theory being proved.

Forensic dispute: James Starrs, the forensic law professor who led the July 17, 1989, exhumation, declared Packer “guilty as sin.” His team reported blunt-force trauma and extensive knife marks, and Starrs believed Packer initially killed the men to steal their belongings before using their bodies as food. The later account in the pile describes three skeletons with defensive hacking marks on the forearms, including Bell’s, suggesting that some victims may have raised their arms against an attacker. That is difficult to reconcile with Packer’s claim that Bell alone became violent and simply killed the others while they slept. The Colorado Encyclopedia’s reconstruction proposes that Packer bludgeoned two men in their sleep, shot others in the hips to disable them, then killed them with a hatchet. It acknowledges, however, that differing decomposition states complicate the theory and that pelvic punctures might be animal marks. Starrs conceded that nobody could directly prove cannibalism: eating human flesh leaves no simple definitive signature, so his conclusion concerned murder, not eating. Walter Birkby, the forensic anthropologist who worked with Starrs, took the opposite position: “We found nothing to corroborate or refute anything Packer said. We’ll never know who did it based on any solid physical evidence.” Michelle Pierce, drawing on archival research, likewise saw Packer less as a calculating killer than a frightened, socially damaged man whose epilepsy and reputation shaped contemporaries’ judgments. The strongest support for Packer came from David Bailey’s separate investigation. A Colt revolver found at the site in the 1950s, rediscovered in a museum collection in 1994, still held three .38-caliber bullets. Richard Dujay’s electron-microscope analysis at Mesa State College matched their lead composition to fragments recovered from Bell’s remains, and a test with a similar pistol produced a hole like the mark in Bell’s hip. That supports Packer’s claim that he shot Bell, but not self-defense or the injuries to the others. Bailey treated it as vindication, but local historian Grant Houston and even Pierce remained skeptical because people routinely found old guns and bullets near the site and claimed them as Packer relics.

Trials and parole: Packer’s legal fate depended as much on credibility and the atmosphere around the case as on the remains. He escaped the Saguache jail in 1874, lived under the name John Schwartze, and was captured in Wyoming on March 11, 1883, after nine years on the run. During the investigation before his escape, he also attempted to attack agency clerk Herman Lauter with a knife, an episode that helped convince General Adams that he was dangerous. At his first trial, Packer rambled for six hours, admitted eating the men, and insisted Bell was responsible for the other deaths. The jury convicted him of premeditated murder and sentenced him to hang, but Colorado’s Supreme Court overturned the conviction in October 1885 because the applicable murder statute had been repealed and could not be applied ex post facto to a pre-statehood crime. At his second trial in Gunnison, on June 8, 1886, the jury convicted him on five counts of voluntary manslaughter, and he received forty years—eight years per victim, then the longest prison sentence in U.S. history. He appealed repeatedly and maintained that he had killed only Bell in self-defense. Polly Pry, the Denver Post reporter whose real name was Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan and who became the paper’s first female reporter, turned that claim into a public campaign after visiting him in prison. She portrayed him as an ex-soldier and victim of circumstance; supporters argued that extreme privation blurred responsibility and insanity. Governor Charles Thomas granted parole, not a pardon, on February 8, 1901, after Packer had served about eighteen years. The sources differ on whether the decisive campaign began with Pry, an earlier petitioner named Duane Hatch, or both. The famous story that Judge Melville Gerry sentenced him with the line about eating five of seven Democrats is apocryphal; the surviving court wording is formal and ends only with “dead, dead, dead.” Packer later worked as a Denver Post guard, prospecting again near Littleton, and died in 1907.

What remains unknown: The decisive piece everyone wants is still missing: a physical reconstruction establishing who struck each blow, when the men died, and whether Bell’s shooting was defensive. No source provides a complete forensic dataset, a conclusive explanation of the pelvic punctures, or evidence resolving the conflicting decomposition patterns. The archive contains confessions, letters, court records, parole files, penitentiary records, and Supreme Court cases, but those records are not examined in full here. No surviving account comes from anyone who witnessed the final camp, and no independent source resolves whether Packer was an incompetent guide whose companions died in catastrophe, a robber who created the catastrophe, or a killer who used genuine starvation to conceal it. The legend remains more complicated than either side’s preferred version: Packer was almost certainly a cannibal, almost certainly lied, and may have killed some or all of the men. The sources do not honestly establish the certainty claimed by either “guilty as sin” or “innocent survivor.”

SECTION 2

The Players

Denver PostDenver newspaper that published Polly Pry’s campaign for Packer’s release

The Denver Post employed Polly Pry, who portrayed Packer as an ex-soldier and common man forced into cannibalism to survive. After Packer’s seventeen years in prison, the newspaper petitioned for his release, and Packer later worked there as a guard. Many believed Pry and her employers helped secure both his release and the job. The paper’s complete historical run is also among the Denver Public Library’s research holdings.

Polly PryDenver Post reporter who campaigned for Packer’s release

Polly Pry partly believed Packer’s account and portrayed him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment who had survived unimaginable horrors. After noticing Hatch’s decade-long petition effort, she visited Packer at the Colorado State Penitentiary in 1899 and launched a media campaign arguing that he had been unjustly tried and convicted. Packer respected her and called her his “Liberator”; many believed her influence helped obtain his release and his later job at the Denver Post. Polly Pry was the pen name of Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan.

Israel SwanElderly member of Packer’s five-man prospecting group and alleged first victim

Packer said Swan died from hunger and exposure, then gave him a rifle before the others abandoned him. In another account, Packer returned from gathering firewood to find the other four men around Swan’s slain body, which Packer said had been struck with a hatchet. He said the men found several thousand dollars on Swan, butchered and ate him, and divided his money. Swan recurs because the conflicting accounts of his death, the rifle, and the missing money are central to the case.

District Court Judge Melville GerryJudge associated with Packer’s 1883 death sentence and its disputed wording

Judge M.B. Gerry sentenced Packer after the prosecution argued that Swan’s remains showed signs of a struggle while the others appeared to have been killed in their sleep. A local newspaper, quoting Larry Dolan, attributed a highly slangy condemnation to Gerry, including references to Democrats and a sentence to hang “dead, dead, dead.” Court records present the sentence in a conventional form. The Colorado Supreme Court later reversed the sentence in 1885 because the applicable law was ex post facto and officially upheld it in 1899.

David BaileyMuseum of Western Colorado curator who investigated a pistol fragment linked to Bell’s remains

In 1994, David P. Bailey found an 1862 Colt revolver while inventorying a historic firearms collection and investigated whether it supported Packer’s claim that he shot Shannon Bell. After a hole was found in Bell’s hip bone during the 1989 exhumation, Bailey suspected it was a bullet hole; the fragment’s chemical composition matched bullets from his Colt. Bailey believed the evidence supported Packer’s self-defense account, although Grant Houston and Michelle Pierce remained unconvinced. In mock trials, juries acquitted Packer more often when Bailey’s evidence was included.

James StarrsForensic-law professor who led the 1989 exhumation of Packer’s alleged victims

James E. Starrs, a George Washington University law professor specializing in forensic science, led the July 17, 1989, exhumation of the five bodies. Starrs and Walter H. Birkby said cannibalism could not be scientifically demonstrated, but Starrs concluded that the evidence was sufficient to find Packer had murdered his companions, probably for their belongings, and then resorted to cannibalism out of necessity. He later said he had proven Packer “guilty as sin.”

Los PiVariant name for the Los Piños Indian Agency, Packer’s 1874 destination

The supplied accounts use “Los Pi” in connection with the Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado. Packer and other prospectors planned to reach the agency before continuing toward Breckenridge. Packer arrived there alone on April 16, 1874, after 65 days, carrying a Winchester rifle, a skinning knife, and a coffee pot with live coals. The agency is where his distressed arrival, questioning, and competing accounts of the journey entered the historical record.

General Charles AdamsOfficer who recorded Packer’s confession and took him for trial

General Charles Adams and his men helped Packer to a table after his arrival at the agency, where he ate so quickly that he vomited. Adams questioned him about the money and belongings he carried, recorded his confession, and had him sign it as a sworn statement. He later led Packer and others into the mountains to search for the bodies, without finding them, and confirmed Packer’s identity before taking him away for trial. Adams also obtained a later admission that Packer had only been a guide and did not know the mountain route.

Colorado State PenitentiaryCanon City prison where Packer was held before his 1901 parole

The Colorado State Penitentiary held Packer after his conviction, where he made horsehair bridles. Polly Pry visited him there in 1899 during her campaign for his release. After pressure from supporters and the Denver Post, the Colorado governor paroled Packer in 1901. The prison recurs as the setting for both his incarceration and the press effort that preceded his parole.

Los PinVariant name for the Los Piños Indian Agency, the prospectors’ planned outpost

The supplied accounts use “Los Pin” for the Los Piños Indian Agency in southwestern Colorado. The prospectors planned to travel there as the nearest outpost before going on to Breckenridge, and Packer and five others left for it on February 9. Packer eventually reached the agency alone, while two men from the river-route party arrived later. The name recurs in accounts of the expedition’s route, Packer’s arrival, and the differing reports of when he reached safety.

Frank MillerMember of Packer’s group and alleged victim whose knife Packer possessed

Frank “Butcher” Miller was one of the five men traveling with Packer. Packer said Shannon Bell killed Miller while he slept, but also said the group later chose Miller as the next person to butcher because he was stocky and had soft flesh. Packer took Miller’s skinning knife, which Nutter noticed; Packer claimed Miller had left it stuck in a tree. Miller’s head was missing from the campsite, and his remains were heavily scavenged.

Gunnison RiverRiver route followed by the prospectors’ alternate party toward the Los Piños agency

Chief Ouray recommended dropping to the Gunnison River and following it north to the agency. The party split, with five men following Oliver Loutsenhizer along the river while six, including Packer, entered the San Juan Mountains; Bob McGrue guided the river-route party until the horses could go no farther. Preston Nutter later reached the agency as leader of that group, and two of its men eventually arrived there. The river also appears in accounts of where Packer became lost and where evidence connected to Shannon Bell was later found.

James HumphreyMember of Packer’s group and alleged victim in conflicting accounts of the deaths

James Humphrey was one of the five men traveling with Packer. Packer first said Shannon Bell killed Humphrey while he slept, and elsewhere said Humphrey was to be sacrificed after Miller; in an amended account, Packer said Humphrey died from exposure to extreme cold. Humphrey’s remains, like George Noon’s, were described as a largely flayed torso attached to skeletal legs, with head injuries suggesting a hatchet. His body was among the five exhumed by James Starrs in 1989.

United StatesCountry whose legal and historical records frame the Packer cannibalism case

The material describes Packer as one of four people historically convicted for cannibalism in the United States and calls the incident the only known U.S. trial associated with human cannibalism. It also notes that cannibalism itself is not illegal in the United States unless someone commits murder to obtain flesh. The case recurs through national reporting, including the United Press International account of Governor Richard Lamm’s refusal of a posthumous pardon, and through annual Packer events held in Colorado and twelve other states.

SECTION 4

The Files

File: The bodies and escape

established

When summer came, General Charles Adams led Alfred Packer and some men back into the mountains to search for and retrieve the bodies, but they found nothing. In August, while Alfred was awaiting trial for manslaughter, illustrator John Randolph crossed the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to the place where Alfred had said he left Shannon Bell, Randolph saw something sticking out of the ground. He smelled a terrible stench and found five men in different states of decomposition. One body was little more than bones, apparently after animals had gotten to it. Two bodies had blunt-force injuries to the head, and Shannon Bell’s body had been stripped to the bones except for the hands and feet and also showed blunt-force trauma to the head. The remains suggested deliberate removal of edible portions rather than animal scavenging, except perhaps in the case of the first body. Randolph sketched the scene and reported it to authorities in Lake City, and a team of 20 volunteers later recovered the bodies. Harper’s Weekly covered the discovery in its October 17, 1874, edition and included Randolph’s illustration; the magazine’s visual treatment helped rivet national attention on the crime.

Other accounts identify him as John A. Randolph, an illustrator for Harper’s Weekly, and place the discovery the following August at the foot of Slumgullion Pass, two miles southeast of Lake City, Colorado, in a pine-shaded gulch above the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River. That place is now colloquially called Dead Man’s Gulch, or Deadman’s Gulch, and the site was five miles beyond town according to another account. The location matched Packer’s original claim that only Bell had been killed there. The snow covering the bodies and campsite had melted during the intervening four months. Randolph sketched the scene and alerted nearby Lake City authorities. The local coroner and law enforcement then went to the site with about 20 volunteers and found all five missing men in various states of decomposition, after four months exposed to the elements and animals. First responders said it appeared that “extreme violence” had befallen them. Frank Miller’s head was missing from the campsite; Miller’s and Israel Swan’s corpses had been heavily scavenged and were little more than scattered bones, and Swan’s skull had a jagged chunk missing. George Noon and James Humphrey were largely flayed torsos of rotting viscera attached to skeletal legs, though their faces remained intact and bearded; Humphrey’s face was slightly more decayed than Noon’s. Noon and Humphrey had received blows to the head that suggested a hatchet, and their bodies had noticeable broken bones. Bell lay with skeletal legs splayed and his arms at his sides. His arms had been crudely cut to the bones while his hands were still fully skinned, and his remaining corpse was a mass of viscera inside an almost wholly flayed torso. His face still had a thick red beard and bushy hair. The lack of noticeable decay in Bell’s face suggested that he was the last to die, and the top of his skull had been ripped open.

The coroner concluded that the men had been killed by blows to the head while they slept. None of the bodies had defensive wounds, and all had similar skull marks. The three bodies that were still intact or partly intact had flesh and muscle cut from choice, meaty locations, but no attempt had been made to consume bone marrow or organs. The men had rags or tattered cloths tied under their rotting feet in place of shoes, suggesting that they had eaten the leather from their footwear after running out of other food. Moldy and tattered blankets lay beneath and beside the bodies. A beaten path led from the corpses to a crude, makeshift shelter used by Packer. Evidence suggested that the deaths occurred before the supplies were totally exhausted, and inside the shelter investigators found possessions belonging to the men that Packer had left behind. Preston Nutter accompanied the party to the site and identified the remains as the five missing men. A rifle broken in two was found nearby; because of the damage on the remains, it was presumed to have been used to bludgeon one or more of the men. Officials buried the remains at the site, then returned to Packer’s makeshift jail to confront him, but he was missing.

The condition and location of the remains contradicted Packer’s version of events. The bodies were all together in one place rather than scattered across miles, and Humphrey and Noon still had large portions of flesh, muscle, and organs that could have been eaten before Bell allegedly tried to murder Packer. The theory at the time was that Packer killed the men for their possessions before supplies ran out, became trapped by snow and weather, and lived for months in his makeshift shelter, walking to the bodies and slicing off meat as he needed it. The area northeast of Lake City where Packer’s party got lost is labeled “Cannibal Plateau” on maps, while the site where the bodies were found is called “Deadman’s Gulch” or “Dead Man’s Gulch”; the lower-grade versions likewise repeat that these names are associated with the case.

The jail was little more than a log cabin on ranch property belonging to the Saguache County sheriff. Months had passed with no definite evidence of a crime, no bodies discovered, and no formal charges against Packer other than the attempt on Herman Lauter’s life. Saguache County authorities were reportedly unhappy about taxpayer money being spent on housing and guarding him. Packer allegedly received a makeshift key for his irons, a penknife, and some food, and escaped easily. Another account says that, before his charge could be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, someone gave him a key, penknife, and food so he could escape. It was never established who helped him; Packer never said who assisted him, how it happened, or why, and it was presumed that his guard had been bribed by Packer or by someone else. He slipped out of his cell and was not seen again for nine years. The accounts variously say he remained on the run for eight years or nearly a decade, but agree that he escaped from the Saguache jail, changed his identity, and was eventually arrested in Wyoming before being returned to Hinsdale County or Lake City for trial. One account says he was living under the alias John Swartze when he was discovered in Douglas, Wyoming, in March 1883.

The generally accepted theory at the time was that Packer had joined the party by overstating his qualifications as a mountain guide familiar with the area and had, at best, led the men to miserable deaths through gross incompetence. A more popular theory said that he had set out from Ouray’s camp with the five men in a premeditated plan to lead them into the wilderness, kill them, and rob them. Nutter and Loutsenhizer tried to discredit Packer’s claimed qualifications as a guide and highlighted his character flaws, multiple stories, and inconsistencies. Local newspapers gave the case constant coverage, with sensational headlines, negative comments about Packer’s character, and imaginative theories that drew national and international attention. Nearly the entire population of Saguache, and soon nearly the entire country and beyond, regarded Packer’s culpability for the men’s deaths as beyond doubt. Cannibalism was not seen as the main issue in his guilt: people already knew the Donner Party story and could understand the need to eat in the wilderness to some degree.

Packer’s later account to General Adams was that he had been gone most of the day searching for food and returned in the late evening. He said he found Bell sitting near the fire roasting a piece of meat cut from Miller’s leg; Miller’s body lay furthest from the fire, down the stream, and his skull had been crushed with the hatchet. Packer said the other three men were lying near the fire with cuts to their foreheads from the hatchet, some having two or three cuts. He said Bell came at him with the hatchet, so he shot Bell, dropped his revolver in deep snow, and lost it. He built a crude shelter from stray logs to fight the snow and wind, then hunkered down for hours when another storm set in. Starving, he decided he had to eat something or die. He said he returned to the fire, covered the men, carried the piece of meat near the fire back to camp, cooked it, and ate it. He tried every day to get away but could not, so he lived off the men’s flesh for most of 60 days. There was also a report that a deer carcass had been found near the campsite, which damaged his claim that wildlife was so scarce that the men quickly had to resort to cannibalism.

The second hearing emphasized that winter travel through the San Juan Mountains was practically suicidal: snow could exceed six feet in a single downfall, while winds and temperatures were severe. Locals had given Packer a safe route beside a main water source that could have provided fresh fish and kept the party on course. Instead, he chose a mountain path with minimal supplies because he believed it would be faster. In fact, the route taken by Packer and his companions was nearly the same length as the recommended route, though less traversable and far more dangerous.

Later investigations left the evidence disputed. James E. Starrs, a professor of law specializing in forensic science at George Washington University, led an exhaustive search and, on July 17, 1989, found the remains near the Lake Fork River upstream from Lake City. The men had been buried only 13 inches below ground at the end of the residential driveway of a home belonging to a local surgeon. Starrs and Walter H. Birkby, a University of Arizona forensic anthropologist who assisted him, said cannibalism could never be scientifically demonstrated because proof would require a picture of the person actually eating human flesh. Packer never denied cannibalism, so it was not the investigation’s main purpose. Starrs nevertheless concluded that Packer had more than likely murdered his companions for their belongings and resorted to cannibalism out of necessity rather than intent. The men were reinterred with proper burial and funeral rites.

The exhumation showed apparent blunt-force trauma to the skulls of two men, with no other noteworthy disturbance apart from butchering. All skulls had damage to varying extents on their upper craniums, and fabric fibers inside some skulls suggested that the men’s heads may have been covered by a blanket at death. The three other skeletons showed defensive hacking marks across the radius and ulna bones of their forearms, including Bell’s skeleton; such marks could have been sustained while shielding the face and body from an attack. Packer claimed Bell had killed the others with hatchet blows to the head, but in his second version he never claimed that he had fought Bell off with the hatchet. All five skeletons had post-mortem injuries, including depressed fractures, butterfly fractures, butchering trauma, and hacking trauma, injuries that seemed to contradict Packer’s claim of minimal cannibalism. Two skeletons other than Bell’s had cylindrical puncture wounds in the pelvic bone. Some investigators have questioned whether the three pelvic marks were bear-scavenging marks or bullet wounds, and no definitive conclusion has been made. One proposed but explicitly plausible scenario is that Packer bludgeoned two men in their sleep, then shot the three remaining men in the hips to incapacitate them; they fought him while he wielded a hatchet, and he killed them with blows to the head before butchering them and using their flesh during the snowbound period and his journey. The differing decomposition states contradict that scenario. It would seem unlikely that Packer shot three of the five in the hip unless he meant to debilitate them before killing them, and further analysis of entry and exit geometry that might clarify the initial cause of death has not been done. Packer’s ultimate motive has therefore remained heavily debated, with several possible theories.

A different report of Starrs’s project said that he described Packer as having “butchered his five fellow prospectors to death and then skinned them for all their bones were worth.” Starrs led a team that exhumed the five victims from a mass grave in the San Juan Mountains the previous July and said the added scientific evidence convicted Packer “beyond any shadow of a doubt,” in his opinion. At a reporters’ gathering, he wore a T-shirt showing five skulls and crossed bones with the legend “Gimme Five! The Packer Project.” That account says Starrs reported that none of the victims had been shot, that four had been killed by hatchet blows to the head, and that the fifth skull had not been found. He said all five sets of bones showed numerous knife marks indicating defleshing, cited “unmistakable proof of cannibalism,” and said Packer used the Colorado winter as a “natural refrigerator,” eating human-flesh filets “morning, noon and night.” Starrs believed the initial motive was to steal the companions’ belongings and that Packer then turned to cannibalism. His stated aim was to settle the debate over Packer’s guilt and “put forensic science on parade.” The project cost an estimated $10,000 to $15,000 and used ground-penetrating radar and laboratory inspection of the remains. It did not settle the spelling of Packer’s first name: Starrs and official court papers used “Alfred,” while Packer signed his name “Alferd.” The first skull uncovered had a gaping hole in its forehead, prompting the sensational report “Professor Exhumes 100-Year-Old Victims of Colorado Cannibal.”

Birkby was less conclusive, saying the evidence neither corroborated nor refuted anything Packer said and that no solid physical evidence would ever show who committed the murders. Lake City’s former town clerk Michelle Pierce, an archival researcher who questioned Packer’s guilt, believes Packer did not murder the five men; her archival research found many details that do not match the official narrative, and she portrays Packer as a pitiable figure whose social problems stemmed from a misunderstood disease and the harsh judgments of contemporaries. Pierce says people disliked Packer largely because they were afraid of him. Grant Houston remained skeptical of the later gun evidence as well.

The Audrey Thrailkill firearms collection at the museum included a Colt revolver reportedly found at the crime site. David P. Bailey’s investigation into the pistol’s background found trial-era documents, including a Civil War veteran’s statement that Bell had been shot twice and the other victims killed with a hatchet. The veteran observed a severe bullet wound in Bell’s pelvic area and a bullet hole through Bell’s wallet. The gun’s accession card said it had been found where Alferd Packer killed and ate his companions. Three .38-caliber cartridges were still loaded in the revolver. Starrs had attributed a hole in Bell’s hip bone to scavenging animal fangs, but Bailey suspected a bullet. Dujay and his team found a tiny fragment of lead in samples from beneath Bell’s remains; spectrographic and chemical analysis matched it to bullets remaining in Bailey’s Colt revolver. Using a similar 1860s pistol, the team fired a bullet into an elk hip bone, and the resulting hole matched the one in Bell’s hip. Bailey believed this supported Packer’s claim that he shot Bell, and it appears certain that at least Bell was shot, but whether he was shot in self-defense remains unanswered. Houston said people had long found old guns and bullets near the massacre site and claimed they belonged to Packer or the prospectors, while Pierce was also unconvinced that Bailey’s pistol was the smoking gun.

The account says that Packer’s life was constantly threatened by nearby townspeople. It also states that no definitive conclusions have been made about the discoveries, including the proposed reconstruction of the killings. Mazzula’s book, *Al Packer, A Colorado Cannibal*, uses archaeology to investigate what happened during the ill-fated journey.

File: The trial and verdict

established

At trial, several parts of Alfred Packer’s story were challenged. People believed the events had been deliberate and premeditated, and it was thought that Alfred had intentionally led the men astray in order to steal their possessions by any means necessary. The prosecution argued that Alfred’s survival story was an attempt to cover up the crime and called many witnesses to support that view. Some witnesses were from the original Utah party. Preston testified that Alfred was always trying to find out how much money the men had, or, as another account puts it, that he had been skulking around trying to learn how much money each man carried. Other witnesses testified about Alfred’s behavior after he reached Saguache and the conflicting stories he told. Otto Mears testified that Alfred had valuable Wells Fargo drafts when he emerged from the mountains, while Constable Herman Lauter testified that Alfred lunged at him with murder in his eyes when ordered to surrender a knife. The prosecution called Otto Mears, Larry Dolan, Oliver D. Loutsenhizer, and Preston Nutter; Preston Nutter served as the prosecution’s key witness. One account says the prosecution called about two dozen witnesses, while the trial narrative says it brought in witness after witness.

The sources give different dates for the opening of the first trial: one says that a trial began in Lake City on April 6, while another dates the beginning to April 9, 1883. Alfred pleaded not guilty. It was presumed that Israel Swan died on or around March 1, and the prosecution said in court that Swan’s remains showed signs of a struggle at death while the others appeared to have been killed in their sleep. When Alfred testified, he spoke for six hours, or, in another account, for more than six hours in a rambling manner. He admitted eating the other party members but swore that he only killed Shannon and that Shannon was responsible for everything else. The jury rejected Alfred’s story and found him guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges. More specifically, Packer was charged with murder, found guilty of the premeditated murder of Israel Swan, and originally sentenced to be hanged; the sources also describe him as eventually tried and convicted of premeditated murder for killing five other persons for their money and “a vicious desire for human flesh and blood.”

The commonly repeated account of Judge M.B. Gerry’s sentence is highly colorful. According to a local newspaper quoting Larry Dolan, Judge Gerry delivered a highly slangy condemnation and sentenced Packer to be hanged by the neck until dead. The reported words included: “Stand up yah voracious man-eatin’ sonofabitch and receive yir sintince. When yah came to Hinsdale County, there was siven Dimmycrats. But you, yah et five of ’em, goddam yah. I sintince yah t’ be hanged by th’ neck ontil yer dead, dead, dead, as a warnin’ ag’in reducin’ th’ Dimmycratic populayshun of this county. Packer, you Republican cannibal, I would sintince ya ta hell but the statutes forbid it.” Another version says Melville Gerry reportedly remarked, “There were seven Democrats in Hinsdale County, and you ate five of them,” followed by, “I sentence you to hang until you are dead, dead, dead as a warning against reducing the Democratic population of the state.” A further reported version has Gerry telling Packer to stand up, calling him a “voracious man-eatin’ sonofabitch,” saying that Packer ate five Democrats after coming to Hinsdale County, and sentencing him to hang as a warning against reducing the Democratic population of the county. It also says that Packer, a Republican cannibal, would be sentenced to hell if the statutes allowed it. The supposed quote is linked to Judge M.B. Gerry, but the Denver Public Library’s history account says the legend that the Lake City judge accused Packer of eating five of the seven Democrats in the county is apocryphal, and historians say that account is not genuine.

Court records present Judge Gerry’s sentence in a conventional, apolitical form. Fred M. Mazzula argues in his book Al Packer, A Colorado Cannibal that Gerry did not actually speak in the Yosemite Sam style of the famous quote. Mazzula used trial transcripts to reconstruct Gerry’s actual statement: Packer was to be removed to the Hinsdale County jail and confined until May 19, 1883, then taken by the sheriff to a place of execution in Lake City and, between 10 A.M. and 3 P.M. that day, hanged by the neck until dead, with God having mercy on his soul. The text says Gerry’s real quote is less colorful but accurate. Other accounts nevertheless say that Judge Gerry sentenced Packer to be “hung from your neck until you are dead, dead, dead,” and that Packer was sentenced to be hanged by the neck until he was dead, dead, dead.

Packer’s lawyers found a technicality before the execution could occur. Before statehood, Colorado Territory did not have a statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder. Colorado became a state in 1876, and the relevant laws were created only after the crime had occurred. The legal sources describe the issue in different but related ways: the murder statutes on the books in 1874 had been repealed and replaced with a “savings clause”; a territorial statute barred the death penalty; and the prosecution’s murder indictments were challenged as having come after a statute of limitations of three years. Packer’s attorney also argued that Packer had not received a speedy trial. In October 1885, the Colorado Supreme Court overturned the murder conviction and scheduled execution because the crime predated statehood and the government could not sentence a man to death for a crime committed before Colorado became a state rather than a territory. This discovery spared Packer from being tried for murder on a technicality, and his death sentence was overturned, allowing him to avoid execution. The sources disagree on the precise legal label, with one describing the ruling as based on an ex post facto law and another calling it a “grandfather clause.”

The overturning of Packer’s murder charge and scheduled execution did not remove his culpability for the men’s deaths. A second trial was held in Gunnison after a change of venue was granted. The venue change was also granted because Packer and his counsel believed that the prejudice and presumed guilt in Lake City—where most people were Democrats—made a fair trial impossible. Of 57 prospective jurors interviewed for the original trial, 54 admitted prior knowledge of the case and 44 said they already believed Packer was guilty. Judge Melville Gerry ordered the sheriff to scour the highways and byways for jurors after the initial pool proved biased. Lake City residents were outraged by the overturned sentence and threatened to hang Packer themselves, so the second trial was moved to Gunnison, about 50 miles away. One account says Packer was incarcerated at Gunnison while awaiting retrial for nearly four years and became a local celebrity during that period.

In the new trial, Alfred again pleaded not guilty and stuck to his story. The prosecution brought in hunters who said there was plenty of food available even in a bad winter. The hunters said game, rabbits, deer, and other food would have been easy to hunt even for someone as inexperienced as Alfred. Local hunters and officials said that although the winter of 1874 was one of the worst they had encountered, the San Juan area where Packer’s party camped still had large game such as deer and antelope, smaller game, and even a deer carcass was reportedly found near the campsite. The prosecution argued that the cannibalism had to have been by choice because food would have been plentiful in the area. It also argued that, at minimum, Alfred led the group astray by taking a more dangerous winter route while posing as a guide. The prosecution’s best-case scenario was that Alfred was extremely negligent.

Packer took the stand in his own defense and asked to be charged the 40 years only for Shannon Bell’s death, saying Bell was the only man he continued to claim he killed; the court denied his request. Accounts differ over the exact result’s legal wording. One says that Packer won a retrial and was eventually sentenced to 40 years in prison on five counts of voluntary manslaughter. Another says he was convicted of involuntary manslaughter charges, while the detailed legal account says that on June 8, 1886, he was convicted of five counts of voluntary manslaughter and sentenced to 40 years in prison. The sentence amounted to eight years for each count, which was the maximum allowed per count, or, in the trial narrative, the maximum of eight years per man. At the time, it was the longest prison sentence ever handed down in United States history, and another source calls it the longest custodial sentence in U.S. history. Packer was sent to serve the sentence at the Canon City, or Cañon City, Penitentiary, and after a confession, a search for the bodies, and a trial, he was sentenced to forty years at the Colorado State Penitentiary. The sources also summarize the outcome by saying that Packer was tried and found guilty of murder in the first trial and manslaughter in the second, and that the incident is the only known trial in the United States associated with human cannibalism. They stress that the modern myth that Packer was convicted of cannibalism is totally incorrect: he was convicted of murder and later manslaughter, not of cannibalism itself.

While imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could and claimed that the sentence was unjust. He claimed that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people, and he sent letters to local newspapers saying that he had been unjustly convicted by an unfair and unsympathetic judicial system and by the ignorant conclusions of small-minded people. Packer filed appeals five times and was denied each time. On June 19, 1899, the Colorado Supreme Court officially upheld Packer’s sentence. One source says Packer went to prison for seventeen years before The Denver Post petitioned for his release; another says that he was paroled after serving 15 years, while the account of his parole says that he was paroled 18 years into his sentence. The sources also disagree about the date, with one giving 1901 and another saying Packer received parole in 1905. The 1901 account says that Colorado Governor Charles Thomas eventually paroled him after a campaign initially led by an old acquaintance, Duane Hatch, and later brought to Polly Pry’s attention. The Denver Post account says that its publishers, Fred Bonfils and Harry Tammen, hired a lawyer to defend him, and that Packer’s lawyer mounted a spirited defense. The sources therefore variously say that Packer spent seventeen years in prison, served 15 years before parole, was paroled 18 years into the sentence, or was released after The Denver Post petitioned for him.

Packer’s story reached a woman named Polly Pry, a reporter for the Denver Post. After hearing Alfred’s story, Polly Pry partly believed him. She wrote stories about him and portrayed him as a man of the people. Polly Pry described him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment and as someone who had survived horrors most people could not imagine. She said his sentence was so harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation. Believing that Packer had been unjustly tried and convicted, she launched a media campaign to bring attention to his plight; in 1899, she visited him at the Colorado State Penitentiary in Cañon City and reported that “the corroding desire for freedom has eaten into his heart” and that “the blind injustice of the world has seared into his soul.” Over time, her stories led local businesses to arrange petitions for Alfred’s release. Another account says he received fan mail from several admiring women while incarcerated and identifies Polly Pry’s real name as Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan, although the assigned account specifically identifies Polly Pry as the Denver Post reporter who championed his cause.

Later investigations have not settled the matter. In the century after the event, several groups performed separate forensic analyses of the remains and compared them with Alfred’s account. Those groups tended to conclude that Alfred was guilty. Some analyses found defensive wounds on bones from the group. One group found marks across the forearms of Shannon Bell, suggesting that he may have defended himself from an attack. In Alfred’s account, Shannon was only shot once and then finished quickly. A 1994 account says that an 1862 Colt revolver found at the site was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and that those bullets matched fragments of lead found in Shandon Bell’s hip; the match suggested that at least part of Alfred’s story may have been true. A separate account says that in the 1950s a rusted 1862 Colt Police Model .32 five-shot revolver was found on Cannibal Plateau with two shots missing. Analysis at Mesa State College’s Electron Microscopy Facility matched bullet fragments exhumed from the burial site to lead from the old pistol. The analysis suggested that Packer did shoot Shannon Bell in self-defense. Another report says that the analysis matched bullet fragments taken from the burial site with lead from the old pistol, while noting that the pistol is now displayed at the Museum of Western Colorado. Museum curator David Bailey said, “Alferd didn’t deny eating the bodies, but he killed only in self-defense,” and said that he was wrongly convicted. At the same time, the forensic account says that whether Bell was actually shot in self-defense remains unanswered, and the text says that no clear or definitive evidence of Packer’s deeds has been found despite in-depth research into proof of them. Thus, the sources include both James Starrs’s 1989 conclusion that Packer was “guilty as sin” and other analyses tending to find him guilty, and Bailey’s view that Packer killed only in self-defense and was wrongly convicted.

Researchers and history buffs are directed to the Denver Public Library as a place to find materials that may prove or disprove parts of the Packer legend. The library holdings include microfilm of Denver and Colorado newspapers from the era, including complete runs of the Denver Post and Rocky Mountain News, as well as copies of Packer’s confession and an unused warrant for his execution, which never occurred. The Colorado State Archives holds several legal and historical records concerning Alfred Packer. The Alfred Packer Collection includes penitentiary records, mugshot photos, parole records, confessions, letters to the Governor concerning Alfred Packer’s parole, a governor’s pardon, original case files from Gunnison and Hinsdale District Court, Gunnison District Court cases 238–241, Hinsdale District Court cases 238–241, original Supreme Court case files, Supreme Court case number 1198 from 1883, case number 1753 from 1885, case number 1980 from 1886, case number 3239 from 1893, and case number 3905 from 1898, as well as military grave registration. The online exhibits page instructs users to click the button below to be taken to the online exhibits, choose “Browse Archive” at the top left below the State Archives logo, and select the Alfred Packer option.

File: The suspicion and confession

established

No one heard from the six men again until Alfred Packer arrived months later at the Los Piños agency. The video says he emerged from the mountains looking unusually well fed for a man who claimed to have been starving: unlike the nearly skeletal wanderers the agency workers had seen before, Packer had a bloated face and a well-fed belly. A biographical account likewise says that, after a little more than two months in the wilderness, he did not look malnourished or threadbare. Packer even reportedly drank whisky for breakfast rather than eating food, although another account says that when he first sat down at the agency table and was given food, he ate so quickly that he vomited.

Packer went to Saguache, where he got a room and a saloon and spent over $100 on drinking and gambling—described by the video as roughly $3,800 in 2023 value—and then spent another $78 in the general store. Witnesses said that, while drinking, he gave conflicting stories about what had happened and seemed to carry a different wallet each time he went out. He never seemed to run out of cash. Packer had sold his rifle at the agency for only $10, which did not explain the rest of the money; the biographical account identifies the buyer as Major Downer, the agency justice of the peace. Packer’s spending was described as frivolous. One account also says that he played high-stakes poker at Dolan’s saloon and bought a $70 horse.

Preston Nutter reached the agency in May as the leader of the other party that had followed the river. Preston later went to Saguache and immediately distrusted Alfred’s story. He told General Adams that the other men would not have left Alfred for dead, since they were prospectors and, even if Alfred was not a good guide, he was better than no guide. Preston also said that the rifle Alfred had sold belonged to an old man in the group, and that the pipe Alfred had left behind belonged to Shannon Bell. Another account attributes those observations to Oliver Loutsenhizer, who told Adams that Packer was not to be trusted and that he suspected Packer’s stories; Loutsenhizer identified the Winchester rifle as belonging to an elderly man in the party and the pipe as Shannon Bell’s. The biographical account additionally says that Packer possessed Frank Miller’s skinning knife and explained it by claiming Miller had stuck it in a tree and walked away without it. Preston pointed out that Alfred had originally joined the group with no money. Witnesses also said that Packer had been trying to find out how much money the men carried, and described him as sulky, obstinate, quarrelsome, and a petty thief willing to take things that did not belong to him. He had a reputation as a scurrilous liar and thief, and as someone most people who knew him disliked and distrusted.

General Charles Adams told the men that he had already met Alfred Packer and that Packer claimed his companions had deserted him. All five men immediately discredited Packer’s account, saying that the men they knew would never abandon someone to die. The men persuaded Adams to send a mounted agency officer to Saguache to retrieve Packer for questioning, under the pretense of recruiting him for a search party. Packer was gathering his things to leave when Nutter and other men approached him again. The agency officer arrived in time and separated the men. The officer told Packer that he had been sent to enlist him as a guide for the search party for the missing men. Packer was reluctant to go but agreed because he saw little option other than vigilante justice, and rode his newly purchased horse back to Los Piños with the officer.

When Packer returned to the agency, he met General Adams and five men he had not seen since February. Loutsenhizer demanded an explanation from him, but Packer repeated the same story he had given the first time. He said he was amazed that the men had not been heard from and worried for their well-being. When asked where his new wealth came from, Packer said that he had received a cash loan from a man in Saguache. Adams said he would send an officer to verify that explanation; the officer returned with reports that Packer had been seen with several different wallets, had told varying stories about his journey, had arrived in Saguache with plenty of cash, and that no one in town claimed to have lent him any money.

Adams and his men asked where Packer had gotten the money, why he had other men’s belongings, and how he had survived the mountains while appearing well fed. Packer first claimed that he had stayed by the fire after getting his feet wet and cold while the others went for food. When they did not return, he said, he assumed they had abandoned him. The story made no sense to Nutter, who doubted Packer’s account and concluded that something wrong had happened. A council was formed to investigate the matter. Adams convened it with himself, Packer, and the agency officers.

As the council was beginning to settle the matter, two Ute men arrived holding pieces or strips of dried flesh they said came from a human found on a hill near the agency while hunting. Packer panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and promised a full confession. As he sobbed, he gave a different account. He reportedly said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.” Herman Lauter, the agency clerk, transcribed Packer’s first official statement, while another account says General Adams wrote down the confession and had Packer sign it as a sworn statement.

In the account given in that first interrogation, Alfred said that ten days into the journey the party ran out of food. The oldest man died first, and the hungry survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they ate him too and found $133 in his pockets. Another man later died while Alfred was away gathering firewood, and the others ate him as well. Alfred said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men. He said that he and Shannon carried some of the bodies’ meat with them for food and covered up the rest. Two weeks later, Alfred said, Shannon tried to kill him; Alfred claimed Shannon had gone mad and attacked him, so Alfred shot him in self-defense.

The fuller statement transcribed by Lauter gives a different and more elaborate version. Packer said the men had left Chief Ouray’s camp with what they thought was enough food for the expected 14-day journey, but that provisions ran out sooner than expected. After days of extreme cold and almost no food, the men started to eye one another. Packer said he returned from gathering firewood to find four men around the slain body of Israel Swan. Swan, he said, had been hit in the head with a hatchet and killed instantly. The four men butchered Swan, and Packer said he accepted the situation and joined them. He said several thousand dollars was found on Swan and divided among the men. They ate the most agreeable parts of Swan’s body, packed some away, and moved on, with Packer taking Swan’s rifle.

Packer said the five men soon ran out of meat again and secretly decided that Frank Miller would be next because he was stocky and had much soft flesh. Miller was butchered and eaten, and Packer took Miller’s knife. Packer said James Humphrey was next to be sacrificed, followed by George Noon. At that point, only Shannon Bell and Packer remained. Packer said that he and Bell swore not to eat each other. Each had a rifle and a couple of thousand dollars of Swan’s cash, and they agreed to say that the four dead men had perished from the elements and had been buried with dignity. They vowed never to speak of the cannibalism and believed that no one would ever think it had been as necessary as they believed it was.

Packer said that after a few days’ travel, with only a rabbit and some roots to eat, they camped near a large lake beside a grove of hemlock trees. Bell later screamed that he could not take it anymore and said that one of them would die for food. Packer said Bell grabbed his rifle and charged at him to bash in his skull. In this account, Packer then butchered Bell, ate as much as he could, packed the rest away, took Bell’s share of Swan’s money, and continued on. He eventually saw the Los Piños agency from a hill and threw away the remaining strips of Bell’s flesh.

Other versions differ even within Packer’s own later statements. In one version, Bell charged at Packer with Swan’s rifle, and Packer shot him. In another, Packer said he finished Bell with a hatchet blow to the head. In a later written account, Packer said he found Shannon Wilson Bell roasting meat over a fire after leaving camp to look for a way out. Bell attacked him with a hatchet, Packer shot him, then took the hatchet and finished him with a blow to the head. Packer claimed he discovered that Bell had hacked the other men to death. He said he and the others had eaten goatskin moccasins and rosebuds and had become weakened, emaciated, and mentally distracted, adding, “Yet if there was any one sane of the six, I was the one.” He admitted that he survived on the men’s flesh until he escaped the mountains, but insisted that he killed only Bell and did so in self-defense. In another account, Packer said that Bell tried to kill him before dying of natural causes so that Bell would not be eaten first; Packer said Bell was killed in a fight and that he then had to eat Bell to survive.

Packer later confessed to living off the flesh of his companions and gave more than one version of what happened. Under interrogation, he admitted to cannibalism but denied murder. He said the men in his party died one at a time and were consumed by the other members until only he and Shannon Bell remained, and he maintained that Shannon Bell had killed the other men. The five original party members said they did not believe any part of Packer’s story. Preston became so angry that he dragged Alfred outside and would have killed him if others had not intervened. Alfred was arrested for manslaughter and imprisoned in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache. Another account says he was jailed at Saguache on suspicion of murdering and stealing from his companions, and that he issued a confession to the crime after a weak story and lack of cooperation.

The story is described as one of the West’s most grisly and enduring legends and murder mysteries. A reference account says that, although no clear or definitive evidence has yet been found, Packer is one of four persons historically convicted for cannibalism in the United States. It says that Packer admitted the small band had starved in the San Juans and that Israel Swan, the oldest member of the group, had died from hunger and exposure. The same account says Packer eventually confessed to having lived off the flesh of his companions while giving more than one version of the circumstances. Another text says it appears likely that Packer killed another prospector in self-defense and then began gnawing on the corpses of those who had already died. A separate account says Packer admitted that the oldest member, Israel Swan, had died from hunger and exposure and that Packer had eaten him.

Cannibalism was and is not illegal per se in the United States unless a person commits murder to obtain the flesh to be eaten. If murder is committed to obtain the flesh, the accused is charged with murder, while the cannibalism itself is charged as desecration or abuse of a corpse. Packer later claimed for the rest of his life that he had been unfairly vilified and convicted for cannibalism rather than murder, which he continued to deny. One account says he was first found guilty of murder in 1883, that the conviction was overturned, and that he was eventually convicted of manslaughter in a second trial and sentenced to 40 years. Another says he was convicted of premeditated murder and sentenced to death. The assigned accounts do not resolve the differences among his several confessions, the competing explanations for the deaths, or whether he killed only Bell in self-defense or murdered the men for their money.

The later accounts also connect suspicion to the missing men’s possessions and money. At the time of Packer’s trial, Israel Swan’s family reported that Swan had gone on the expedition with about $6,000 in cash and gold and had a valuable Winchester rifle. Swan was 65 years old when he died. The money and rifle would have given Packer a strong motive for murder. The other four men may have been complicit in Packer’s murder and later betrayed by him, or they may have been murdered because they were witnesses. Packer was not found with any gold when arrested, and although he had money left, it did not amount to thousands of dollars. The prosecution argued that the only logical reason for Packer to attempt such a perilous journey through the mountains with so little food and supplies was to lead the men into the wilderness to kill and rob them. Authorities accused him of murdering the other men, and local authorities were not convinced by his story.

Packer later fled. He approached Cabazon while trying to buy supplies, and Cabazon reported him to the local sheriff. The sheriff apprehended Packer and contacted General Adams. Packer said he had fled because he feared mob justice from the people of Saguache. Because the actual crime was committed in Hinsdale County rather than Saguache County, Packer was sent to Lake City for detention and prosecution. When Adams asked why Packer had not told this story nine years earlier, Packer said he had been excited and that the story that first came to mind was the one he told. The account of his capture says that Cabazon encountered him on March 11, 1883, when Packer was using the alias John Schwartze and trying to buy supplies; Packer was arrested and taken to Denver, where he signed a second confession on March 16. He said his main reason for fleeing had been fear of mob justice from Saguache.

Packer remained known as Alfred or Alferd Packer, the Colorado Cannibal, and local papers dubbed him the “Man-Eater.” He emerged from the woods with a pocket full of cash and no traveling party, and his contradictory confessions, the belongings of the missing men, his spending, and his reputation for lying and theft all contributed to the suspicion that he had murdered them. More than a century after he was first accused of killing and dining on five fellow prospectors, forensic law professor James Starrs said that he had proven Packer was “guilty as sin.” Starrs’s team exhumed the five victims’ bodies and reported that none had been shot, four had been killed by hatchet blows to the head, and all five sets of bones showed knife marks indicating “defleshing.” Starrs said the evidence proved cannibalism and argued that Packer’s motive was initially to steal his companions’ belongings before turning to cannibalism. Those later forensic conclusions were presented as evidence against Packer, but the assigned accounts also preserve his repeated claim that he killed only Shannon Bell, and did so in self-defense.
