File: The expedition

established

The sources describe the expedition as a journey toward newly found goldfields near Breckenridge, Colorado, after news of a gold strike and rumors of great fortunes. One account says Robert, or “Bob,” McGrue organized 20 people to travel from Salt Lake City to the San Juan Mountains after hearing of gold discovered in Breckenridge; another says a party of 20 left Utah, while a separate account calls the expedition a party of 21 that departed Bingham Canyon on November 8, 1873. The men were largely strangers, united by the hope of becoming rich. The video says they left Bingham Canyon on November 20, 1873, and that the group first encountered Alfred about 25 miles into the journey south of Salt Lake City. George Tracy instead said that the party met the 23-year-old Alfred Packer near Provo. Alfred asked where they were going, said he wanted to join them, and claimed to be both a prospector and a guide who knew the territory between Utah and Breckenridge, or the San Juan territory, well. Because he had no provisions, he offered $25 to join the band. The prospectors needed a guide and accepted his help, although they initially hesitated because he seemed odd. Members of McGrue’s party later said that Packer may have overstated, or even fabricated, his familiarity with the area. He reportedly left without a rifle and had only a Colt revolver. The video says Alfred had actually worked as a guide for a few months, but had no idea where he was going; he habitually got lost, argued with clients, stole from people, and lied. Other accounts likewise describe Packer as greedy with rations, lazy, obstinate, and constantly fighting, and say he was obsessed with how much money the other members carried. He quarreled constantly with Frank “Butcher” Miller. At Packer’s first trial, Preston Nutter called him a “whining fraud,” and Packer’s epileptic seizures made his presence in the group strenuous. Rumors also circulated that he had spent time in jail in Salt Lake City on a charge of murdering a hunting partner.

The biographical account says that when he was younger, Packer served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War. He enlisted on April 22, 1862, in Winona, Minnesota, in Company F of the 16th Infantry Regiment, and was honorably discharged eight months later because epilepsy had triggered seizures. He enlisted again on June 25, 1863, in the 8th Iowa Cavalry Regiment at Ottumwa, Iowa, but was honorably discharged on April 22, 1864, after another seizure-related episode. After the discharges, he worked driving horses and other draft animals across the West, and also worked as a hunter, a range hand, and a laborer or odd-job worker for mining companies. He tried mining in Colorado, but his bad attitude meant that he was constantly fired.

The first roughly 260 miles were already difficult. The trail was covered in heavy snow, which hid the path, crippled the wagons and horses, and made the wagons move slowly. The party traveled more slowly than expected toward Breckenridge despite Packer being their guide. For a time they relied almost entirely on a compass, but they became lost anyway, ultimately because of Packer’s inexperience. One account says that Packer’s ineptitude led the men through the San Juan Mountains for nearly two months, covering only 250 miles at an average of three miles a day. By January, their provisions had run out. They first ate horse feed and then neared the point of considering the horses themselves as food. The men later described Alfred as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting.

On January 21, the party reached a Ute encampment in a valley just outside Montrose, in the Uncompahgre Valley. The accounts call Chief Ouray “the White Man’s Friend.” Ouray led the Utes, supplied the men with food and lodging, and gave them shelter. He urged them to stay until spring or until the weather improved, offering to share what he and his people had with them. He warned that no Ute would attempt the journey in those conditions and that trying it meant certain or almost certain death. The group still had roughly 120 miles to travel and the San Juan Mountains to cross. By February the weather had not improved, and Ouray again said that the safest choice was to accept his offer and wait out the winter. One account says some of the men paid Ouray a trespassing fee and camped with the Utes for the rest of the winter, while others accepted a week’s provisions and traveled to the Los Pinos Indian Agency in Saguache County. Another says that, after the party met, the men decided to leave half the party behind with the horses and wagons until spring while the other half went to the agency. A further account says that 11 men decided to continue: they would first reach the Los Piños, or Los Pinós, Indian Agency, the closest outpost, and then proceed to Breckenridge. These accounts therefore differ on the party’s total size and on how many continued, but all say that the men feared other groups would reach the gold first and ignored or resisted Ouray’s advice to wait.

Ouray gave the departing men food and safe directions for bypassing the mountains. He said the best route was to drop down to the Gunnison River, follow it north, and then reach the agency. Alfred insisted that crossing the mountains directly would be better, more direct, quicker, and preferable to going around. Five men believed him and went with him. In the account identifying the factions, five men followed Oliver Loutsenhizer along the Gunnison River, while six, including Packer, headed through the San Juan Mountains; Loutsenhizer threatened to shoot Packer if Packer tried to follow the river group. In another account, on February 9 Packer and five others left for the Los Pinós Indian Agency, which was said to be 75 miles ahead. The five-man group with Packer consisted of George “California” Noon, Israel Swan, James Humphrey, Frank “Butcher” Miller, and Shannon Wilson Bell. Noon was a teenager, while Swan was elderly and rumored to be carrying thousands of dollars in cash. The fact that no one in the other group opposed Packer’s departure led many researchers to conclude that his inexperience and attitude had become too taxing and that they thought they were better off without him. A separate account says that five prospectors, carrying a week’s worth of provisions, followed Packer southeast and then south along the Lake Fork on February 9, passing the site that would become the townsite of Lake City within six months.

The expedition’s leader, Bob McGrue, initially guided Packer’s men along the river route recommended by Ouray until his horses could go no farther. McGrue then offloaded the men’s provisions and walked or led the horses back to the Ute camp. It is thought that Packer’s party continued farther down the river and then took a path high into the mountains. When McGrue turned back, he knew the party lacked enough supplies to reach the agency, but he had had enough of arguing with Alfred. After the drop-off, the men had only about 14 days of food, no adequate winter clothing, no snowshoes or flints, hardly any matches, and, in the more specific account, no flint at all. They carried only a few rifles—elsewhere described as two rifles—one pistol, a hatchet, a couple of knives, and minimal ammunition. They therefore entered the mountains with barely enough food for the supposed 14-day journey on the safest route and without the equipment needed for a winter crossing. Packer later wrote that Ouray told them they could reach the agency on foot across the mountains in no more than five days. The source says this part of Packer’s account was not entirely truthful: Ouray never told him they were only five days from the agency, because three or four feet of snow blocked the way. Men who stayed at the camp said Ouray told the prospectors they would all die and that none of his men would show them the route because they were afraid of the deep snow. When Packer’s party nevertheless decided to enter the storm, Ouray gave them provisions. Packer wrote that the fare was scanty—about 20 pounds of flour and no more than 10 pounds of good meat—and that Ouray drew a crude map on the ground with a stick and gave them all the directions he could.

The group without Alfred followed the river and endured brutal winter conditions. Their food ran out before they reached the agency, and cowhands eventually found them and fed them at a cattle camp until spring. In April, when the weather improved, four men reached the agency in May; in the more detailed account, two of the five river-route men arrived first and the remaining three, including Loutsenhizer, arrived a few days later. Alfred had already reached the agency and left before them. According to the expedition’s leader, Packer’s party followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther, after which the leader unloaded their provisions and walked the horses back to Ouray’s camp. The leader knew at the time that the men did not have enough supplies to reach the agency.

The sources present differing summaries of what followed. One says that, after fierce snowstorms boxed in the party, many men returned home but six, including Packer, continued; another says that six prospectors, including Packer, chose to leave the Utes, lost their way in the San Juan Mountains, and became snowbound. A further account says that five prospectors—Noon, Bell, Humphrey, Miller, and Swan—followed Packer, while broader summaries describe the six men crossing the rugged San Juan Mountains during the winter trip. Nothing was heard from the six prospectors for nearly three months. In mid-April, only Packer emerged from the mountains alive; the text says that five men died agonizing deaths in the mountain cold and that a sixth man’s life was irrevocably altered by the events. Packer was the only survivor of the trip.

The foundation’s account presents Packer’s cannibalism story as highlighting the dangers faced by nearly every nineteenth-century prospector who ventured into the Rocky Mountains, while also describing the episode as one of the West’s most grisly and enduring legends and murder mysteries. The prospectors were traveling after reports of a gold strike and “marvelous tales of enormous fortunes.” By late January, they had run out of provisions and were eating livestock feed when they reached Ouray’s encampment. Ouray gave them food and shelter and warned them to stay for the winter, but six prospectors—Swan, Noon, Miller, Humphrey, Bell, and Packer—chose to continue. The party became lost, cold, and hungry without proper provisions or equipment. One account says that Packer led the men through the mountains for nearly two months and covered only 250 miles at an average of three miles a day; another says they were lost and snowbound until only Packer emerged in mid-April. The account describes the six as eventually discovered by warpainted Ute Indians, who brought them near Ouray’s village, where they made a makeshift camp. Ouray exchanged food and supplies with them and advised them again to shelter there until winter passed. The contingent wanted to reach Breckenridge before thousands of fortune hunters arrived, first reaching the Los Pinos Agency and then continuing to the goldfields.

The sources do not give one uncontested version of Packer’s experience after he left Ouray. Packer later said that the men’s provisions were exhausted after three or four days, that they cooked and ate rawhide goatskin moccasins, and that they gathered and stewed rosebuds where snow had blown away from wild rose bushes. He also described surviving on roots, pine gum, and occasional rabbits. The video says that he ate rabbits, roots, and rosebuds for months afterward and that his experience as a guide was what got him out alive. The accounts state that he left Utah with few provisions and no weapons, although he later arrived at the Los Pinós Agency with a Winchester rifle, a skinning knife, and a coffee pot containing live coals. He became snowbound and struggled through the mountains in inadequate clothing, without snowshoes, almost no matches, no flint, and with only two rifles, one pistol, a couple of knives, a hatchet, and minimal ammunition. Packer later gave multiple accounts of the deaths. In the story recorded in one source, Bell attacked him with a hatchet while roasting human meat, and Packer shot Bell and finished him with a blow to the head. In another version, Packer said Bell killed the entire camp while he was away scouting and that Packer shot Bell when Bell rushed at him. The sources leave open whether the men died from exposure and starvation, whether Packer killed one or more of them, and whether the deaths involved self-defense or greed.

The two river-route groups eventually reached the Los Pinós Agency and decided to assemble a search party for the missing men’s remains. Two Ute men said that a place like the one Packer described existed about 50 miles away across the hills. The search party was led by agency clerk Herman Lauter and included five Utah miners, several agency officers, and Packer as guide. After two weeks, near the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, Packer said he was lost and did not recognize the area. Nothing was found, and the party returned to the agency. On the way back, Packer tried to murder Lauter with a knife. He was caught, restrained, and arrested. General Charles Adams had been willing to believe Packer until the attempted attack on his officer convinced him that Packer was dangerous. The sheriff took Packer to Saguache and jailed him outside town, in a log cabin, for his own protection. Cabazon, who had been part of the original party that left Provo, had stayed with the Utes and later safely reached the destination with Bob McGrue and Preston Nutter’s party.

The sources say Packer emerged at the Los Pinós Agency on April 16, 1874, after nine weeks or 65 days, during a fierce snowstorm. He was disheveled and distressed, with rags over his feet instead of shoes, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from one side, and a rifle over the other; he begged for food and shelter. He was later described as suspiciously well fed and flush with cash. He reportedly spent over $100 on liquor and gambling, or played high-stakes poker at Dolan’s saloon and bought a $70 horse. Preston Nutter said Packer had been skulking about trying to discover how much money each man carried. Packer’s possession of a rifle belonging to one of the missing men and his possession of other property further aroused suspicion. The sources also disagree about the money: one says Packer had several hundred dollars or valuable Wells Fargo drafts, while the reported value of Swan’s money ranged from $133 found in a dead man’s pocket to about $6,000 in cash and gold. Packer had reportedly sold his rifle at the agency for $10, which did not explain the rest of the money. The five original party members said they did not believe any part of his story and told General Adams that the men they knew would never have abandoned another man to die. They pointed out that the Winchester rifle Packer carried had belonged to an elderly member of the group and that a pipe he left at the agency belonged to Shannon Bell.

The sources say that Packer’s later cannibalism story is presented as a dramatic account of the expedition’s dangers, while the underlying expedition facts are found in the historical and biographical accounts. Those accounts say that the story became a notorious legend, but that no clear or definitive evidence resolves whether Packer killed his companions or merely ate those who had already died. The text says that only Packer survived, that five men died agonizing deaths in the mountain cold, and that their deaths and the events permanently altered the sixth man’s life.

The source further characterizes Packer as having a habit of getting lost, arguing with clients, stealing from people, and lying. It says that the group that accepted a week’s provisions from Chief Ouray and traveled to the Los Pinos Agency nearly perished after losing its way in the harsh mountain wilderness.

File: Alfred’s Later Life and Legacy

established

After prison, Alfred worked for a while as a guard at The Denver Post and later as a ranch hand. Many people believed that the Denver Post position came directly from Polly Pry and her employers helping to secure his release. Packer retained lasting respect for Pry and called her his “Liberator.” Another account says that, after prison, Alfred moved to Denver but found city life intolerable, then moved a few miles out to Littleton to be closer to the mountains. In Littleton he bought a copper mine, or copper claims, and returned to prospecting until epilepsy overcame him. People described him after prison as kind, modest, and charitable, in contrast to the grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy man they associated with his earlier life. He was also described as rich with stories and liked by children. He lived modestly and was reported to be charitable. Rumor said he had become a vegetarian by the time he died.

The accounts disagree about the length of Packer’s imprisonment and the circumstances of his release. One says he went to prison for seventeen years before The Denver Post petitioned for his release; another says he had served 18 years of his 40-year sentence. Other accounts say he served 16 years of the 40-year sentence, was released, and lived out the rest of his life in relative peace, while another says he served 15 years and was paroled. Packer made many appeals for a pardon after entering prison, but they were repeatedly refused. Duane Hatch petitioned for Packer’s release for nearly a decade before Polly Pry noticed his effort. Pry, a Denver Post reporter, used Packer’s Army service to portray him as a common man who had been caught in a regrettable situation, forced to resort to cannibalism to survive. Her stories helped change the minds of local businesses and people sufficiently that petitions and requests reached Colorado Governor Charles Thomas. Thomas initially faced strong opposition but ultimately relented. The account says that his last official act before leaving office was to parole, but not pardon, Packer, on the condition that Packer would not try to profit from his story. Packer never obtained an official state pardon for his crimes, although another account says Pry’s campaign and a retrial eventually led to a pardon on January 7, 1901. A separate report says that Governor Richard Lamm declined Packer’s posthumous pardon request in 1981; at a 1982 bust unveiling, Lamm said, “Well done!” to sculptor Tom Miller while making a pun-filled refusal of an unconditional pardon.

In the penitentiary, Packer made horsehair bridles, including one displayed at the Museum of Western Colorado in Grand Junction, and he also built elaborate Victorian dollhouses. A fuller account says he often made leather belts, bridles, wooden canes, and watch fobs from dyed and braided horsehair, normally selling them as souvenirs to visitors and occasionally giving one to someone he considered special. He gave Rebecca A. Newman a chain bracelet as a sign of affection and a desire for a relationship, while also hoping through their correspondence to learn what she could do for him. Packer wrote that he would make Newman proof that he was worthy of aid from philanthropic people and those better situated than he was financially and otherwise. The text says women like Newman still exist today and can play a dangerous game when contacting famous criminals who are experienced manipulators.

Packer’s death is also described differently in the sources. One account says he died peacefully in 1907 at age 65, at a ranch near Deer Creek in western Jefferson County; another says he died two years after his 1905 parole at that ranch. The death record cited the cause as “Dementia – trouble & worry,” although his clinical cause of death has been described as a stroke. Another account says he died alone in 1907 in Littleton, Colorado, at age 69, while a biographical entry lists his lifespan as 1842–1909. Packer was buried in Littleton, Colorado, and his grave has a veteran’s tombstone listing his original regiment in 1862; the tombstone is a replacement because the original grave marker was stolen. The Littleton Cemetery Association cemented over the grave in 1973 to deter grave robbing and vandalism. Visitors have left offerings including a toy firetruck, a marijuana vape pen, and a vase for flowers, and a wooden bench invites visitors to sit and reflect. On the day one narrator visited, cemetery sprinklers sprayed directly onto the memorial bench; the narrator interpreted this as another joke on the Colorado Cannibal.

The authenticity of Packer’s remains is disputed. Edward Meyer of the Ripley’s Believe It or Not! Museum said the museum possessed Packer’s dissected skull and had bought it from an anonymous party for a reported $20,000. No statement was made about how the skull’s authenticity was verified beyond the seller’s information about its origin being considered sufficient. If the skull belongs to Packer, his head is presumed to have been removed shortly before or after burial, dissected with the brain removed for study, and preserved by arsenic curing. The skull is said to have passed to a traveling sideshow, then to a private party, and then to Ripley’s; as of 2008, it was reported to be at the Ripley’s Museum in San Antonio, Texas, after being moved from the New Orleans facility following Hurricane Katrina. These claims conflict with the belief that Packer’s corpse is intact.

Packer’s misspelled name and unique reputation, the historical account says, live on, and he evolved from Old West infamy to New West celebrity. His pistol is now displayed at the Museum of Western Colorado. In Lake City, “Al Packer Days,” the Packer Burger at the Cannibal Grill, and a large wooden historical marker for the Alferd Packer Massacre Site are popular attractions. Travel magazines say the Hinsdale County Museum has “the largest collection of Packer memorabilia known,” including skull fragments and clothing buttons from victims, as well as shackles used when Packer was imprisoned. Tourists are advised not to miss the actual burial site, five minutes from town. Lake City now treats Packer as both its patron saint and its antihero. The town sits at an elevation of 8,661 feet and has only a few hundred residents, and some visitors come to the Colorado Rockies town hoping to see Al Packer’s ghost. Local businesses include the Packer Saloon & Cannibal Grill and the Cannibal Cabins. The town has hosted annual Al Packer Day events featuring coffin races, mystery-meat eating competitions, and a look-alike contest.

Grant Houston, head of the Hinsdale County Historical Society and editor-publisher of the Lake City Silver World, says many local people believe Packer was guilty. Houston says locals believed Packer lured the men into the mountains, killed them, and took off with what he coveted. The courthouse walls display Packer memorabilia, including newspaper accounts and trial records. Residents of Lake City, Boulder, and other Colorado towns held mock trials for Packer, and when David Bailey’s evidence was included, jurors acquitted Packer more often than not. Packer remains a popular figure in Colorado state history. A restaurant in Boulder, Colorado, called the Alferd Packer Grill was named in his honor, and events and traditions honoring him take place annually in Colorado and 12 other states. The University of Colorado Boulder has an Alferd Packer Grill about 40 miles from Packer’s grave. It greets students with a giant portrait of the cannibal and the slogan “Have a friend for lunch!” UC-Boulder students have hosted Al Packer Days while wearing shirts with slogans such as “Finger lickin’ good” and “When you care enough to eat the very best.”

In 1968, students at the University of Colorado in Boulder renamed the student-union restaurant the Alferd E. Packer Memorial Grill. Students could order an “El Canibal” beefburger, and a giant map outlining Packer’s travels through Colorado was displayed on the wall. The grill has since been renamed the Alferd Packer Restaurant & Grill. In 1998, James E. Bank wrote Alferd Packer’s Wilderness Cookbook. In 1977, Secretary of Agriculture Bob Bergland attempted to terminate a contract for the department’s cafeteria food service but was prevented by the General Services Administration. To embarrass the GSA, Bergland and his employees held a press conference on August 10, 1977, unveiling a plaque naming the executive cafeteria “The Alferd Packer Memorial Grill” and announcing that Packer’s life exemplified the spirit and fare of the cafeteria and would “serve all mankind.” Barbara Walters covered the event on ABC Evening News. The stratagem succeeded, and the contracts were terminated soon afterward. Bergland later removed the plaque after accepting the bureaucratic objection that it lacked official GSA authorization. The plaque is now displayed on the wall of the National Press Club’s The Reliable Source members-only bar, where it also serves as a memorial to USDA employee Stanley Weston, who lived from 1931 to 1984. The National Press Club’s hamburger is called the Alfred Packer Burger.

CU film students Matt Stone, a CU film student involved in Packer’s retelling, and Trey Parker, a CU film student involved in Packer’s retelling, later created the television show South Park. They produced Cannibal! The Musical in 1993; it was Trey Parker’s directorial debut. The text says the film was short-lived, like Packer’s companions. The film was released exclusively to Boulder, Colorado, in 1993 and to the rest of the United States in 1996. Phil Ochs, the songwriter behind Packer’s ballad, wrote “The Ballad of Alferd Packer” in 1964. Ochs used humor in the song, which fits the lighthearted attitude toward Packer and his alleged crimes, but the song never appeared on any of Ochs’s studio or live albums, instead appearing on compilations issued after his death in 1976, most recently on the 2010 compilation On My Way. C. W. McCall wrote “Comin’ Back for More” about Packer. In Dashiell Hammett’s novel The Thin Man, Nick Charles advises Gilbert Wynant to read a selection about Packer’s expeditions. That selection, from Thomas Samuel Duke’s Celebrated Criminal Cases of America, gives Packer’s first name as Alfred. Packer is also the subject of Harold Schechter’s true-crime book Man-Eater.

The sources describe Packer as Alfred, or Alferd, and also as John Schwartze and the Colorado Cannibal. He was an American prospector and self-proclaimed wilderness guide, one of three children born to James Packer and Esther Packer, née Griner. By the early 1850s, his father had moved the family to LaGrange County, Indiana, where he worked as a cabinetmaker. Packer is said to have had a bitter relationship with his parents. In his late teens he moved to Minnesota and worked as a shoemaker. He was a Civil War veteran who enlisted in the Union Army, but epilepsy triggered frequent seizures and he was honorably discharged eight months later; another account records an enlistment on April 22, 1862, in Company F of the 16th Infantry Regiment, a discharge eight months later, a second enlistment on June 25, 1863, in the 8th Iowa Cavalry Regiment, and a second discharge on April 22, 1864. Packer suffered from epilepsy from an early age, and the stigma of the condition followed him throughout his life.

After the war, Packer traveled west and worked numerous jobs over the next nine years, including hunter, wagon teamster, ranch hand, and field worker. His seizures and overall attitude meant he never kept a job for long. He worked for a couple of months as a guide, but people who knew him later said he was ill-suited to the role and prone to losing his way. He worked mining-related jobs from mine to mine but never found prosperity in mining; he worked briefly as a miner in the Colorado Territory and then moved to the Utah Territory. Most people who knew him disliked and distrusted him because of his argumentative personality, nearly pathological lying, and reputation for theft. His first name is listed as Alfred, and he is known to have used both Alfred and Alferd in life.

Packer’s later celebrity also fits the pattern described by mental-health professionals as hybristophilia, the disorder of becoming infatuated with jailed serial killers and mass murderers. In popular culture, it is called Bonnie and Clyde syndrome. The condition is usually characterized by a woman communicating with a high-profile criminal in an attempt to kindle a relationship. Alfred Packer, also spelled Alferd, received fan mail from several women while incarcerated for his crimes. Before Polly Pry helped secure his release, he received a constant stream of curious visitors who came to ogle Colorado’s nationally known prisoner, as well as many letters from adoring well-wishers. One sympathizer was Mrs. Rebecca A. Newman. By opening communications with Packer, Newman apparently hoped to form a friendship and express sympathy for his circumstances. When Governor-Elect Alva Adams learned of Newman’s affection for Packer, he warned her in writing against defending him or excusing his conduct, but Newman insisted that communications be opened anyway. She asked Packer for a full, detailed statement of the circumstances connected with his most extraordinary trials and sufferings.

Packer’s case reflects the eagerness of prospectors to trespass into the Ute reservation and illustrates how swiftly development took place once the San Juan region opened. The case attracted national and international attention to Lake City and its environs. Although modern myth states that Packer was convicted of cannibalism, the historical account says this is incorrect: he was tried and found guilty of murder in the first trial and manslaughter in the second. One account says he served 16 years of his 40-year sentence before being released and living out the rest of his life in relative peace; another says Packer served 15 years and was paroled. Packer died peacefully, but his legacy has been anything but settled, and his story has remained the subject of historical and popular discussion ever since. The text says that the story people know about Alferd Packer and the story that actually occurred are not always the same, and that Packer ultimately found some redemption from the people of Colorado, or at least from the justice system.

In her 1899 report after visiting Packer at the Colorado State Penitentiary in Canon City, Denver Post writer Polly Pry wrote that “the corroding desire for freedom has eaten into his heart” and that “the blind injustice of the world has seared into his soul.” Packer’s supporters also signed a petition calling for his pardon.

File: Alfred’s final account

established

The historical account says that on March 11, a man calling himself John Schwartze approached the shopkeeper to buy supplies for a planned trip. The shopkeeper thought the man looked familiar and realized that he was Alfred, not the John Schwartze he remembered from years earlier. He told the local sheriff that he had spotted a criminal, and Alfred was arrested and taken to Denver. General Adams confirmed that the man was Alfred and took him away for trial; he then asked Alfred again what had really happened years earlier. Alfred gave what would be his final version of events, and the account says he adhered to it until his death.

In that final version, Alfred said the party had left Chief Ouray’s camp with only enough food for one grown man for a week. After two or three days, they were hit by a brutal snowstorm. They reached the base of a mountain and then crossed a deep valley where the snow was so deep they could barely walk. They moved to higher ground, and by the fourth day had only about a pint of flour left. For roughly ten more days, Alfred said, they survived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge. Several men cried out every night and prayed to God to escape alive. The group eventually crossed the main ridge and camped beside a river. They followed the stream for a day until they reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal.

Alfred said they tried to cross the lake to reach trees that could provide shelter, while exhaustion and tension grew. According to his account, Shannon Bell became furious with Alfred for getting them lost and with the others for seeming pathetic. Bell then told Alfred to scout higher on the mountain for a way across. Alfred took a pistol and found only steep slopes and more snow. He admitted to General Adams for the first time that he was only “kind of” a guide: he did not really know what he was doing and did not know that side of the mountains.

When Alfred returned, he said he found Shannon eating a piece of meat beside the fire. He saw one man lying near the fire, then saw the other three men lying around it and not moving. Alfred said Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet when he approached, so he shot Shannon in the stomach and finished him off after he fell. Alfred later wrote that the night after Shannon’s death was the worst night of his life. In a later letter, he said he was surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.” He felt himself losing his sanity and beginning to understand Shannon. In another letter, he wrote, “The greatest wonder is that I ever returned to a rational condition.”

The next morning, Alfred tried to follow his tracks from the day before but turned back because of the snow and exhaustion. He built a small shelter from wood and branches, but it did not satisfy his hunger. He decided that hunting was not a reliable food source. The relief of eating, he said, overcame the horror of what he was doing, and he decided what he had to do to survive. He then spent another two months in the shelter living off the rest of his party. Sixty days later, he saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind. He took this as evidence that he was in Slumgullion Pass, known for its yellow color. Alfred then realized where to go and set off up the mountain again in early spring.

Before leaving, he gathered some remaining meat to eat while walking. He checked the other men’s pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache. He had also eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth and sometimes had to stop when they began freezing; when that happened, he lit a fire to warm them. Near the agency, he ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some that were later found by Utes. He said he tried to stop the Utes from going farther. Alfred said he had wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but did not want to be reminded of the horror he had endured.

Alfred said he escaped and fled trial because he feared a mob would get past his guard and kill him. He had nearly been killed by Preston Nutter and believed that someone would eventually finish the job. After escaping, he went to Arkansas under a false name and worked on a ranch, then moved to Arizona, and finally went to Cheyenne, where he was found. The account says Alfred consistently told this final story until his death.

The historical material also preserves several accounts that Packer gave after being recaptured, and they do not all match. In one version, Packer said Shannon Bell killed James Humphrey, George Noon, and Frank Miller while they slept around the campfire. Packer said he had been out searching for food when he returned to camp and Bell confronted him with a hatchet. He said he fired twice with a pistol and shot Bell in self-defense. After killing Bell, Packer said, he lived on the flesh of the dead men for most of the sixty days he was out. He said he tried to get away every day but could not.

During detention, Packer retracted his earlier account of the events leading to the deaths of the five men. He then said the party encountered a strong blizzard in the mountains; the snow fell so heavily and persistently that they became hopelessly lost and could not retrace their steps. Provisions were already minimal and quickly ran out. They also ran out of matches and had to carry hot embers in a steel coffee pot to light fires. Days passed without game, attempts at ice fishing failed, and the men roasted and ate their shoes and tried to survive on scant edible vegetation. Packer said they made a pact that if one died, his meat would help save the others from starvation. After days of hiking with almost nothing to eat, Israel Swan could go no farther. The group found a pine-shaded gulch beside a lake and set up camp, and Packer said Swan later died of hunger and exposure.

In Packer’s signed first confession, he said Old Man Swan died first and was eaten by the other five people about ten days after they left camp. He said Humphreys died four or five days later, was eaten, and had about $133; Packer found Humphreys’s pocketbook and took the money. He said the butcher was later killed while carrying wood and was eaten. In the same confession, Packer said Bell shot “California” with Swan’s gun and that Packer killed Bell by shooting him. He said he covered the remains, took a large piece with him, and traveled fourteen days to the agency. He also said Bell wanted to kill him with his rifle and struck a tree, breaking the gun.

In Packer’s later amended version, the men endured almost 20 days from Ouray’s camp and more than 10 days without substantial food. Packer said James Humphrey died of exposure to extreme cold, while George Noon was killed days later by Shannon Bell solely for food. In this version, Bell later rushed at Packer with his rifle and intended to bludgeon him with the stock. Packer said he took valuables from the dead men because they no longer needed them, but made no statement about the exact items or the amount of money taken. While he was in jail, observers challenged his credibility. Packer confessed to taking the deceased men’s valuables on the ground that they no longer needed them.

Cabazon was summoned to Cheyenne, confirmed Packer’s identity, and accompanied him by train to Denver for a second confession, which Packer signed on March 16. In that confession, Packer said the party had asked him to climb a nearby hill to see whether he could see anything farther away that might help them navigate. He said that after a full day of going up the hillside and coming back down, he returned to camp and found that Bell had killed the entire camp and was eating the leg of a man roasted in the campfire. Packer said Bell rushed at him, and he shot Bell through the stomach with the rifle he had taken on the hillside. His third confession included more details but largely the same information as the second.

Packer wrote in a letter that his comrades were dead and that he was left alone amid starvation and utter isolation, with his weak body and mind driven toward irrationality. Throughout his incarceration, he maintained that he was innocent and had acted only in self-defense when attacked. He complied with questioning and repeated his story of self-defense and cannibalism for survival. In another letter, Packer wrote that after nine days the last provisions had been eaten, and that the group ate goatskin moccasins and subsisted on rosebuds until they were weakened, emaciated, and mentally “completely distracted.” The text calls that claim ridiculous because Packer had been living in a different territory and under an alias to evade capture.

File: Alfred Packer’s arrival and first story

established

The video account says that two months after six men entered Colorado’s San Juan Mountains in winter, only one man emerged, and he looked weirdly fed rather than emaciated. That man was Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal. On the morning of April 16, 1874, he arrived alone at the Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado, although another historical account says that nine weeks after leaving Utah he reached the agency south of present-day Gunnison. He came through a snowstorm with rags on his feet instead of shoes, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging on one side, and a rifle on the other; another account lists what he carried as a rifle, a knife, a steel coffee pot, and a satchel, while the historical account says the coffee pot contained live coals. He begged the agency staff for food and shelter. General Charles Adams had his men help him to a table, but Packer could not keep the food down: he ate so fast that he vomited, and later said that prolonged near-starvation had altered his digestion. Though haggard and worn, he was otherwise fit. The agency men thought it odd that someone lost in the wilderness for a little over two months did not look as malnourished and threadbare as most lost wanderers they had seen; his face was reported as bloated rather than gaunt. Packer also said that he would drink whisky for breakfast instead of eating food.

Over whiskey, Packer said that the others had become too exhausted to continue, that he had suffered snow blindness and frostbite, and that they had left him behind to fend for himself. He said he had been hired by five men to guide them to Breckenridge, became snow-blind during the journey, lagged behind, and became a burden to the party. He claimed that Israel Swan gave him a rifle before the others decided to abandon him. Packer said he survived alone on roots and rosebuds, ate his moccasins, and lived for months on rabbits, roots, and rosebuds. In a later statement, he said that three or four days after their provisions ran out, they cooked their raw-hide moccasins; that their trail was entirely drifted over; and that they gathered buds from wild rose bushes, stewed them, and ate them. After arriving at the agency, he claimed that his comrades had left him while they searched for food and said he did not know what had happened to his companions, even though he carried large sums of their money and a rifle known to belong to one of them.

Packer said he was broke and sold the Winchester rifle in his possession to Major Downer for $10. He stayed at the agency for ten days before going to Saguache to buy supplies for the trip back to Pennsylvania. There, he bought a horse for $70 and booked a room at Dolan’s Saloon, where he played high-stakes poker. Larry Dolan later claimed that Packer spent around $100 during his stay and even offered to lend him $300. Packer spent another $78 at Otto Mears’ general store, and it was also claimed that he possessed several different wallets. Another member of the original gold seekers confronted him about where he had obtained the money he was spending. One account describes Packer as coming out well fed and flush with cash, spending more than $100 on booze and gambling while seeming uninterested in food, and becoming evasive when questioned about the other men.

Preston Nutter later arrived in Saguache with two other original party members and met Packer in Dolan’s Saloon. Nutter asked where the rest of the party was, and Packer said he had gotten his feet wet and frozen. Packer said they had camped when a winter storm began, that he had started a fire while the others went ahead to look for food, and that Swan had left him with his rifle in case of trouble but never returned. Packer said he then made his way through the mountains, eating mainly rosebuds and small animals. Nutter found the story odd because Packer looked well-fed and because it seemed unlikely that five miners unfamiliar with Colorado would abandon their guide in snowbound mountains. Nutter also thought it strange that Swan would give Packer his rifle, leaving four men with only one rifle for hunting. He noticed that Packer possessed a skinning knife that had belonged to Frank Miller; when asked about it, Packer said Miller had stuck it in a tree and walked away without it.

In his first confession, Packer said that the first two deaths were circumstantial, given the rough conditions, and that everyone took part in cannibalism to stay alive. He said one man was “killed accidentally” while collecting firewood. He also said that Shannon Bell killed a man he called “California,” after which Packer killed Bell in self-defense and traveled for 14 days back to civilization. These details formed part of Packer’s first of several contradictory accounts, while his initial story at the Los Piños Agency was that his companions had abandoned him and that he did not know what had happened to them.

File: Polly Pry

established

Polly Pry was the pen name of Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan, a reporter known for her connection to the case of Alfred Packer. She was born into a wealthy family in 1857 and, at age fifteen, eloped to Mexico with the railroad industrialist George Anthony. Five years later, she left Anthony and moved to New York to become a reporter. The New York Times initially rejected her, although she later obtained a trial assignment and secured a full-time job there. In 1898, Frederick Bonfils hired her for The Denver Post, making her the paper’s first female reporter. She was also a member of the Denver Woman’s Press Club.

In the early 1900s, news reporter Polly Pry launched a journalistic campaign to release Packer, whom the Denver Public Library History account calls “The Colorado Cannibal” and presents as one of the most notorious and most misunderstood tales in Colorado history. That account says Pry first met and interviewed Packer while researching an article about Colorado’s prison system and the Colorado State Penitentiary. The popular journalist championed Packer’s cause while he was in prison, believed he was innocent of murder, and advocated for him in print throughout his trial. In her column, she argued that since sailors were legally allowed to eat people if they were lost at sea, the same rules should apply to people stranded in the mountains. Because her Packer column increased The Denver Post’s revenue and readership, she persuaded its owner, Harry Tammen, to pay for Packer’s defense and demand a retrial. Denver Post publishers Fred Bonfils and Harry Tammen also hired a lawyer to defend Packer. Her advocacy helped win Packer’s release. The Denver Public Library History account says the retrial eventually led to a pardon on January 7, 1901; the biographical account, meanwhile, says Pry met Packer in 1901 and advocated for him throughout the trial.

Packer became the sole survivor of a six-man party that tried to travel through the San Juan Mountains of the Colorado Territory. His account of the campsite events remained roughly the same as his second official version. The account of Packer describes him as having eventually confessed to living off the flesh of his companions while giving more than one version of the circumstances, and says he maintained during his incarceration that he had acted only in self-defense. The story of Alferd Packer, “The Colorado Cannibal,” is presented as one of the most notorious and most misunderstood tales in Colorado history.

After the trial, Pry was present during a confrontation between Packer’s attorney and the owners of The Denver Post. The Post’s owners learned that the attorney had taken a double payment and demanded that he return the money. During the confrontation, attorney W. W. Anderson pulled a gun and shot both men. As Anderson prepared to shoot again, Polly Pry jumped in front of Harry Heye Tammen to try to shield him. Anderson threatened to shoot her if she did not move, but she stalled Anderson long enough for the police to arrive. She used her skirt to stop the bleeding. Rumors later circulated that her skirts had saved her publishers’ lives by slowing bullets from the gun.

When union workers boycotted The Denver Post over her stance on labor issues and immigration, she founded her own paper, Polly Pry. After she founded her own paper, gunmen attacked her in her home rather than her workplace. She was a strong advocate of free speech and, during World War I, came to the aid of French war orphans.

Two film versions of the Alfred Packer story included Polly Pry. In Jim Roberson’s The Legend of Alfred Packer (1980), Cynthia Nessin portrayed her. The film included the confrontation with Anderson, but Anderson was not named and was credited as “Gunman.” After Pry begins telling Packer’s story, she does not appear again, and the shooting is not mentioned again. The Legend of Alfred Packer depicted her as hard-drinking and forceful. In Trey Parker’s Cannibal! The Musical, Toddy Walters played Polly Pry. That film went more deeply into her involvement with the Packer case, but ignored the fact that she was married in order to make her a love interest for Packer. The biographical account says Pry was said to have gotten her nickname because fellow reporters believed she could pry information out of anyone.

Alferd Packer survived winter starvation in the San Juan Mountains by resorting to cannibalism after extreme deprivation.

Held across: SRC_2.

Full case, both sides
Case for the claim

The case for the claim is that Alferd E. Packer survived an extreme winter ordeal in the San Juan Mountains by eating his dead companions. In February 1874, six men set out across the mountains in the middle of winter toward newly discovered goldfields, with roughly 120 miles and the San Juan range still ahead of them. Packer, a prospector who lived from 1842 into the early twentieth century—reported variously as dying in 1907 or 1909—became famous after confessing that he had eaten comrades who died while the group was trapped. The 10th Grade, 8th Grade, and 4th Grade accounts all repeat the association between the prospector born in 1842, the February 1874 expedition, and cannibalism. His enduring reputation as someone known for cannibalism supports the account that, after severe deprivation, he resorted to consuming the dead in order to survive. SRC_2

Case against the claim

The case against the claim is that the episode may not have been a straightforward instance of starvation cannibalism. The available account says it appears likely that Packer killed another prospector in self-defense and only afterward began gnawing on the corpses of men who had already died. Packer himself said that he fired twice with a pistol and shot Shannon Bell in self-defense, and the analysis likewise suggested that he did shoot Bell in self-defense. His lawyer mounted a spirited defense, but Packer was eventually tried, convicted of premeditated murder, and sentenced to death. His reported appearance also cuts against the picture of a man reduced by extreme starvation: his face was described as bloated rather than gaunt. Thus, although Packer was known for cannibalism, the evidence can be read as indicating violence followed by eating corpses, rather than survival by cannibalism after extreme deprivation; the account remains contested.
